title: Güvenlik Ürünü Kendini Koruyamazsa: Endpoint Central Ajanı ile Sorumlu İfşa Hikâyem
summary_en: A vulnerability in ManageEngine Endpoint Central allowed local administrators to bypass 'Self-Defense' protections and uninstall the security agent by manipulating MSI and Registry components.

lesson.cause: The security agent relied on user-mode protections (software-level checks) to prevent its own removal. Because these checks did not operate at the Kernel level (the core part of the operating system that controls everything), a user with Local Administrator privileges (a high-level account) could directly modify the Windows Registry (a database of system settings) and MSI (Windows Installer) components to bypass the uninstallation password and self-defense logic.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify the target software version installed on the machine.
Version: v11.4.2516.37.W
Why: Knowing the exact version helps determine if known protections are present (a version is a specific release of software).

DISCOVERY
2. Confirm that security features are active in the management console.
Settings: Self-Defense and Uninstall Password Protection
Why: These features are supposed to prevent any user, even an administrator, from removing the agent without a secret code.

3. Attempt a standard uninstallation through the Windows Control Panel.
Why: This confirms the 'Uninstall Password Protection' is actually prompting for a password as expected.

EXPLOITATION
4. Target the Windows Registry, which is a central database for system and app settings.
Registry: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Why: The researcher identified that the agent's protection logic relied on specific keys in this database (a key is like a folder in the registry).

5. Target the MSI (Microsoft Installer) components of the agent.
Component: MSI Database
Why: MSI is the standard format Windows uses to install/uninstall software; manipulating its cached data can trick the system into ignoring protection rules.

6. Perform 'interventions' on these components to disable the self-protection logic.
Payload: [Researcher withheld specific commands for safety]
Why: By modifying the registry or MSI records, the researcher could tell the system that the agent is allowed to be removed without a password.

7. Trigger the uninstallation process again using system tools.
Command: msiexec /x {Product-Code}
Why: Using the command-line installer (msiexec) with the 'uninstall' flag (/x) allows bypassing the standard user interface (UI).

IMPACT
8. Verify the agent service is no longer running.
Why: Once the agent is gone, the organization loses its ability to manage patches (software updates) or enforce DLP (Data Loss Prevention - tools that stop data theft).

9. Observe that security policies like 'Device Control' are no longer active.
Why: This proves the machine is now 'blind' and unprotected from the central security team.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional security app 'GuardDog' on target.example. GuardDog has a setting 'BlockRemoval=1' stored in the Windows Registry at 'HKLM\Software\GuardDog'. When you try to uninstall it, the app checks this value. If a user with Local Admin rights runs a script: 'reg add HKLM\Software\GuardDog /v BlockRemoval /t REG_SZ /d 0 /f', they change the value to 0. Now, when the uninstaller runs, it sees '0' and allows the removal without asking for the administrator's password. This works because the app trusted a registry key that the local admin could change.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs in security software, always test if 'Tamper Protection' can be defeated using native OS tools like Registry Editor or MSIExec. A common mistake is assuming that requiring 'Local Admin' privileges makes a bug 'not a vulnerability'; however, for security products (EDR/DLP), their primary job is to remain active even if a local admin (or malware with admin rights) tries to kill them. Look for settings stored in locations that the OS allows an administrator to modify.
lesson.fix: The fix is to move protection logic from 'User Mode' to 'Kernel Mode' using a driver. A Kernel driver can intercept any attempt to modify the agent's files or registry keys and block them at the system level, regardless of the user's permissions. In version 11.5.2605, the vendor added 'Prevent Agent Data Tampering' which uses this kernel-level protection. Users must enable this in 'Agent Settings -> Agent Protection Settings'.

title: How I Hunt for Information Disclosure Bugs: My Complete Bug Bounty Methodology | by Samadhan…
summary_en: The researcher details a methodology for discovering Information Disclosure vulnerabilities by analyzing API responses for excessive data, inspecting client-side JavaScript for secrets, and triggering error messages to reveal internal system architecture. This approach identifies instances where applications inadvertently leak sensitive data like internal IDs, PII, or configuration details to unauthorized users.

lesson.cause: The root cause is often 'Excessive Data Exposure,' where developers return full database objects to the frontend and rely on the user interface to filter what is visible. This occurs because it is easier to code a generic 'select *' query than to specify individual fields for every API endpoint (a specific web address where data is exchanged). Additionally, security misconfigurations like leaving debug modes enabled or failing to remove source maps (files that map compressed code back to readable code) allow internal logic to be exposed. Finally, a lack of strict authorization checks allows users to access data belonging to others by simply guessing their ID.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECONNAISSANCE
1. Open Burp Suite, a tool used to intercept and inspect data moving between your browser and the website.
2. Browse the target website normally to capture all background traffic.
3. Identify all API endpoints, which are URLs used by the application to fetch data (e.g., /api/v1/user/profile).

CLIENT-SIDE ANALYSIS
4. Open the browser's Developer Tools (F12) and navigate to the 'Sources' or 'Debugger' tab.
5. Search through JavaScript files for keywords like 'API_KEY', 'secret', or 'internal' to find hardcoded credentials.
6. Check if the application loads '.map' files, which are files that reveal the original, uncompressed source code of the application.
7. Inspect 'localStorage' and 'sessionStorage' in the browser to see if sensitive tokens or user data are stored insecurely on your computer.

API EXPLOITATION
8. Locate a request in Burp Suite that retrieves user information, such as:
GET /api/v1/account/settings HTTP/1.1
9. Examine the response body, which is the data the server sends back, usually in JSON format (a text-based way to organize data).
10. Look for 'hidden' fields that the website doesn't show on the screen, such as 'is_admin: false' or 'internal_db_id: 5521'.
11. Attempt to change the ID in the request to see if you can view another user's data (IDOR):
GET /api/v1/account/settings?id=1002 HTTP/1.1
Why: This tests if the server checks if you own the data you are asking for (Authorization).

ERROR AND DEBUG PROBING
12. Send invalid data to an endpoint, such as putting a word where the app expects a number:
GET /api/v1/product/abc HTTP/1.1
13. Analyze the error response for a 'stack trace,' which is a detailed report of the server's internal code execution path.
14. Check for common debug paths like '/actuator/env' or '/phpinfo' which might be left open by mistake.
15. If a debug interface is found, look for 'environment variables,' which are settings that often contain database passwords or secret keys.

IMPACT ASSESSMENT
16. Document how the leaked information (like an internal file path or a private email) could be used to launch a more dangerous attack.
lesson.example:
Suppose a fictional site 'target.example' has a profile page. When you view your profile, your browser sends this HTTP request (a message asking for data):
GET /api/users/me

The server responds with this JSON (data format):
{
  "username": "hunter1",
  "bio": "Hello world",
  "internal_password_reset_token": "9922-8811-X",
  "last_login_ip": "10.0.0.5"
}

While the website only displays the 'username' and 'bio' on the screen, the server is leaking a 'password_reset_token' and an internal IP address. An attacker can see this hidden data by using a proxy tool like Burp Suite. The attacker could then use that reset token to take over the account because the server sent too much information to the browser.
lesson.takeaway: Always look at the raw data returned by the server, not just what appears on the webpage. Use Burp Suite's 'Target' tab to find all JavaScript files and search them for secrets or internal URLs. A common variant of this bug is 'BOLA' (Broken Object Level Authorization), where changing a number in a URL reveals someone else's private data. Avoid the mistake of thinking a bug is 'low' severity just because it's an error message; if that message reveals a database version, it helps an attacker choose the right exploit later.

Information disclosure is one of those vulnerability types. A small detail in an API response, an exposed configuration file, a debug message, or an old backup file can reveal information that should not be publicly accessible. In this article, I will explain the methodology I use to approach inform

title: Breaking into a Major Bank
summary_en: Exposed Spring Boot Actuator endpoints allowed the researcher to download a full memory heapdump, revealing plaintext credentials and internal secrets. This misconfiguration in a major bank's production environment led to a $4,800 bounty reward.

lesson.cause: The root cause was the failure to disable or secure Spring Boot Actuator endpoints in a production environment. These endpoints, specifically `/actuator/heapdump`, are designed for internal monitoring and debugging but were left publicly accessible without authentication. Furthermore, the application's default error pages leaked its underlying framework (Spring Boot), allowing the researcher to fingerprint the technology stack and target known sensitive paths.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher started by performing directory enumeration (using a tool to guess common folder names) on the bank's main website.
2. They discovered two hidden endpoints: `/error` and `/health` (specific web addresses where an application receives requests).
3. By visiting `/error`, the researcher observed a specific JSON (a data format) structure and timestamp format.
4. They recognized this specific error layout as a 'fingerprint' (identifying software by its unique behavior) for the Spring Boot framework (a popular tool for building Java web apps).
DISCOVERY
5. To confirm the presence of more hidden management tools, the researcher ran Nuclei (an automated scanner that looks for known vulnerabilities).
6. The scanner identified several exposed 'Actuator' endpoints (tools in Spring Boot used to monitor and manage the application).
7. The researcher checked `/env` (an endpoint that shows environment variables) but found no immediate secrets there.
8. The researcher then identified the `/actuator/heapdump` endpoint as being publicly accessible.
EXPLOITATION
9. The researcher sent a request to download the heapdump file (a snapshot of everything currently stored in the computer's memory/RAM by the application).
GET /actuator/heapdump HTTP/1.1
Host: bank.example
Why: This request triggers the server to generate and send a large binary file containing the entire state of the application's memory.
10. Once the file was downloaded, the researcher used the `strings` command (a tool that finds and prints readable text inside binary files).
strings heapdump_file_name
Why: Even if a file is mostly computer code, 'strings' extracts human-readable text like passwords or API keys that were temporarily stored in memory.
IMPACT
11. By searching through the extracted text, the researcher found sensitive internal secrets and the 'flag' (proof of access).
12. The researcher confirmed that while data might be encrypted in a database, the JVM (the engine running the Java code) must decrypt it into plaintext (unencrypted text) to use it, making it visible in the heapdump.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site 'shop.target.example' built with Spring Boot. A researcher notices that visiting a non-existent page returns a 'White Label Error Page'. They immediately try to access 'https://shop.target.example/actuator/env'. The server responds with a JSON object containing 'SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: "super-secret-db-pass"'. This happens because the developers forgot to set 'management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=*' in their application configuration, allowing anyone to see the server's private environment variables.
lesson.takeaway: Always fingerprint the technology stack by looking at error messages and headers; a 'White Label Error Page' is a massive signal for Spring Boot. Once identified, immediately check for common actuator paths like /env, /heapdump, /trace, and /mappings. Use automated scanners like Nuclei with specific 'misconfiguration' templates to find these quickly across large attack surfaces. A common mistake is assuming that because /env is masked or empty, the other endpoints are safe; always check /heapdump as it contains decrypted secrets from the application's runtime memory.
lesson.fix: To fix this, developers should restrict Actuator endpoint exposure in the 'application.properties' or 'application.yml' file by only enabling necessary, non-sensitive endpoints. Ideally, all management endpoints should be moved to a different port or protected behind strict authentication using Spring Security. To disable all web exposure, use: 'management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=*'. To only allow health checks, use: 'management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info'.

title: From Shodan to an Unpaid Delivery: How a Chain of Weaknesses Led to Real-World Impact
summary_en: A chain of vulnerabilities involving a predictable OTP and a lack of server-side payment verification allowed researchers to order and receive physical products for free.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by two primary failures: first, the use of a hardcoded or predictable OTP (One-Time Password) value of '1234' in a UAT (User Acceptance Testing) environment exposed to the public internet. Second, the application's backend (the server-side logic) failed to independently verify payment status, instead trusting a client-side 'success' signal from a demo payment gateway to mark orders as paid and initiate shipping.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Use Shodan (a search engine for internet-connected devices) to find IP addresses (unique numerical labels for computers) associated with the target domain.
2. Access the discovered IP address directly in a web browser to reveal a functional application.
DISCOVERY
3. Identify the login page which requires an OTP (One-Time Password - a temporary security code).
4. Test the predictable value '1234' in the OTP field.
1234
Why: The developer used a simple, easy-to-remember code for testing that was never removed (a hardcoded credential).
5. Navigate through the application to find a link to a separate retail UAT (User Acceptance Testing - a sandbox for testing new features) environment.
6. Attempt to log in to the UAT environment using the same '1234' OTP bypass.
EXPLOITATION
7. Browse the e-commerce section of the UAT site and add a physical product to the shopping cart.
8. Proceed to the checkout page and select the company's internal payment option.
9. Observe the redirect to a demo bank interface provided by Razorpay.
10. Click the button labeled 'Success' on the demo bank page.
Why: This demo page is meant for developers to simulate a successful transaction, but it should not be connected to real shipping workflows.
IMPACT
11. Observe the application backend processing the order as 'Paid' based on the demo result.
12. Track the order through the shipping provider (Delhivery) to confirm a real product is being delivered.
Why: The system failed to perform server-side verification (checking with the bank's actual records) before fulfilling the order.
lesson.takeaway: Always perform 'Recon' on IP addresses found via Shodan, as they often host 'shadow' or UAT environments with weaker security than the main domain. Look for predictable patterns in OTPs or default credentials in non-production environments. A critical lesson is that payment status must never be determined by the client's browser; always use server-to-server webhooks (automated messages between servers) to confirm financial transactions. A common mistake is assuming that because a site is a 'test' site, it cannot trigger real-world actions like shipping.

Opening it directly in a browser revealed a fully functional application that appeared identical to the website accessible through the target’s domain. title: CoRover.ai leaked two million phone calls. Yours might be one.
summary_en: CoRover.ai left an Azure Blob Storage container publicly accessible, exposing two million private phone call recordings, financial spreadsheets, and support tickets to anyone with a web browser.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a misconfigured Azure Blob Storage container (a cloud-based folder for storing files) that lacked any authentication (a way to prove who you are). CoRover.ai failed to implement access control lists (rules defining who can see what) on their storage environment. This allowed anyone with a web browser to view and download sensitive files without a password. The article notes that while the company held security certifications like SOC 2 and ISO 27001, these audits did not ensure the actual technical implementation of storage security.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Researchers identified CoRover.ai as a major provider of AI-driven phone assistants for banks and retailers.
2. They discovered an Azure Blob Storage bucket (a cloud storage container) belonging to the company.
DISCOVERY
3. The researchers attempted to access the storage URL directly through a web browser.
https://[account-name].blob.core.windows.net/[container-name]
Why: They wanted to see if the Public Access Level (a setting that allows anyone on the internet to view files) was set to allow anonymous viewing.
4. The browser successfully listed the contents of the container, confirming it was publicly accessible.
EXPLOITATION
5. Researchers browsed the directories and found approximately two million audio files.
6. They identified that these audio files contained full recordings of conversations between customers and AI assistants.
7. They located additional folders containing screenshots of support tickets (digital records of customer issues).
8. They found spreadsheet files containing financial statements and revenue data.
IMPACT
9. The researchers confirmed the data included names, dates of birth, and financial details.
10. They realized the audio could be used for voice cloning (using AI to mimic a person's voice) to bypass bank security.
11. They attempted to report the leak to CoRover.ai's privacy contact but received no response.
12. They reported the issue to CERT-In (a national computer emergency response team) but were ignored for months.
13. They finally messaged the CEO on LinkedIn, after which the bucket was secured (made private).
lesson.example: Imagine a company called 'HealthBot.example' that stores patient voice memos in an Amazon S3 bucket (a cloud storage service). They name the bucket 'healthbot-patient-memos'. If they set the bucket policy to 'Public,' anyone can visit 'https://healthbot-patient-memos.s3.amazonaws.com' and see a list of all files. An attacker could then download 'memo_123.mp3' and hear a patient's medical history. This happens because the 'Block Public Access' setting was disabled in the cloud console, allowing the browser to fetch the data without an authentication token (a digital key used to prove identity).
lesson.takeaway: This is a classic 'Open Bucket' vulnerability, which is common in cloud environments like AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. Hunters should look for company names or subdomains in cloud storage URLs during recon (the process of gathering information about a target). A key signal is finding a URL ending in '.blob.core.windows.net' or '.s3.amazonaws.com'. A common mistake is assuming that because a company has security certifications (like ISO 27001), their technical assets are automatically secure. Always verify the 'Public Access' settings on any cloud storage discovered.
lesson.fix: The fix is to disable public access at the storage account level and use Shared Access Signatures (SAS - temporary, secure links) or Azure Active Directory (a system for managing user identities) for authorized access. Developers should implement the 'Principle of Least Privilege' (giving only the minimum access needed). In Azure, this means setting the 'Allow Blob public access' property to 'Disabled' in the storage account configuration. Additionally, companies should use automated tools to scan for publicly exposed buckets continuously.

title: From an Android APK to Production MQTT: Exposed Credentials in Attendo (formerly Petpooja Payroll)
summary_en: Hardcoded production MQTT credentials found within an Android APK allowed unauthorized access to sensitive employee PII, including names and photos, and the ability to send commands to payroll devices.

lesson.cause: The developers bundled production environment configuration files (.env/production.json) directly into the Flutter assets of the mobile application. These files contained static, shared credentials (username and password) for a production MQTT broker. Because the broker did not enforce granular, per-user permissions, these shared credentials granted full access to sensitive messaging topics across the entire organization.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher obtained the Attendo Android APK file, which is the package format used to install apps on Android.
2. They used extraction tools to look inside the app's internal folders, specifically targeting the assets directory.

DISCOVERY
3. Inside the folder 'resources/assets/flutter_assets/.env/', they located several configuration files.
4. They opened 'production.json', a file used to store settings for the live version of the app.
5. Inside this file, they found a plain-text username and password for an MQTT broker, which is a server that manages messages between devices.

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher used a standard MQTT client tool to attempt a connection to the server address found in the file on port 1883.
7. They provided the extracted credentials to the broker.
8. The broker accepted the credentials, completing 'authentication' (proving who you are).
9. The researcher then performed a 'wildcard subscription' using the '#' symbol.
Why: In MQTT, '#' is a wildcard that tells the server 'send me every single message from every possible channel' (topic).
10. The researcher began receiving 'heartbeat' messages, which are automated signals devices send to say they are online.

IMPACT
11. They observed 'punch-in' messages containing 'Emp_id' (Employee ID) and 'Ename' (Employee Name).
12. They found 'base64_string' fields in the messages.
Why: Base64 is a way to represent binary data, like images, as a long string of text characters. 
13. By converting that text back into an image file, the researcher could view actual photographs of employees taken during attendance.
14. They discovered 'device passwords' being sent in plain text through synchronization messages.
15. Finally, they tested 'publishing' a message to a topic.
Why: Publishing means sending a message to the server that other devices will receive, potentially allowing an attacker to fake attendance records or trigger device actions.
lesson.example: Imagine a smart-lock company called 'SecureHome'. They release an Android app that contains a file named 'config.json' inside the APK. Inside that file is: {"mqtt_host": "broker.target.example", "user": "admin_app", "pass": "SuperSecret123"}. An attacker extracts the APK, finds these credentials, and connects to broker.target.example. They subscribe to the topic 'homes/+/commands'. Because the broker doesn't check if 'admin_app' should only talk to one specific home, the attacker sees every time someone unlocks their door and can even send a '{"action": "unlock"}' message to any house in the system.
lesson.takeaway: Always assume that any secret stored inside a mobile app (APK or IPA) is public information. Attackers will routinely use tools like 'apktool' or simply unzip the app to find '.env', '.json', or '.xml' files containing API keys and passwords. To find these, search for keywords like 'broker', 'mqtt', 'key', or 'password' within the extracted assets. A common mistake is thinking that 'authentication' (logging in) is the same as 'authorization' (having permission to see specific data); even with a valid login, the server must restrict what data that specific user can access.
lesson.fix: Never store shared production credentials in a client-side application. Instead, use a 'Token Exchange' pattern where the app authenticates the user against a secure API, which then provides a short-lived, unique token or X.509 certificate for the MQTT broker. On the broker side, implement 'Access Control Lists' (ACLs) to ensure that a device or user can only subscribe to or publish to topics specifically belonging to them (e.g., 'user/123/#' instead of '#').

The initial finding was straightforward: the APK contained a username and password for a production MQTT broker. The more interesting part came during validation. The credentials were accepted by the broker, and the authenticated session provided access to messaging channels carrying employee attendance information, device telemetry, and configuration data. title: Turning the Valve - Exploiting RCE and LPE in the Steam Platform
summary_en: A technical analysis of Remote Code Execution (RCE) and Local Privilege Escalation (LPE) vulnerabilities discovered within the Steam platform.

lesson.example: We assume a fictional website at target.example allows users to test their connection. An endpoint (a specific web address used to interact with a service) takes a parameter (a piece of data sent to the app) called 'ip'. Vulnerable Code: system('ping ' + ip). Attack Request: https://target.example/test?ip=1.1.1.1;id. Why: The semicolon (;) is a character that tells the computer to start a new command (an instruction for the operating system). By adding ';id', the attacker sends a payload (malicious data designed to exploit a bug) that forces the server (a computer hosting the app) to run the 'id' command. This is Remote Code Execution (RCE), which is the ability to run any code on a remote computer. This happens because the app does not check if the 'ip' contains dangerous characters before using it.

title: I Got Invited to a Private Bug Bounty. The Bug Was Sitting in a JavaScript File.
summary_en: An AWS Cognito Identity Pool ID found in a public JavaScript file allowed unauthenticated users to obtain temporary AWS credentials with excessive permissions, enabling the listing of private customer documents in an S3 bucket.

lesson.cause: The root cause was an overly permissive Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy attached to the 'Unauthenticated' role of an AWS Cognito Identity Pool. Developers often grant broad permissions (like s3:*) to guest roles during development to ensure features like 'sample previews' work, but fail to restrict these permissions to specific file paths or actions before moving to production, effectively granting any internet user access to the entire storage bucket.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Read the program scope document to identify allowed domains and testing boundaries.
2. Open the target web application in a browser and activate Developer Tools (F12) to monitor network traffic and loaded resources.
3. Locate the main JavaScript bundle, which is a large file containing the code that runs the website's interactive features.
DISCOVERY
4. Search the JavaScript bundle for keywords like 'identityPoolId', 'region', or 'bucket' to find cloud configuration details.
5. Identify the AWS Cognito Identity Pool ID, a public identifier used to request temporary cloud credentials.
'us-east-1:xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx'
Why: This ID is intended to be public so the app can ask AWS for temporary keys to perform tasks like fetching images.
6. Formulate a hypothesis: If the app allows guest users to see samples, the 'Unauthenticated' role might have broad permissions.
EXPLOITATION
7. Use the Amazon Cognito API to request a unique Identity ID for your current session.
8. Use that Identity ID to request temporary AWS credentials, including an Access Key, Secret Key, and Session Token.
9. Configure the AWS CLI (a command-line tool for managing cloud services) with these temporary credentials.
10. Run the 'get-caller-identity' command to verify the active role and confirm you are acting as a guest.
aws sts get-caller-identity
Why: This command returns the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the current user; it confirmed the researcher was using the 'Cognito-Unauth-Role'.
IMPACT
11. Attempt to list the contents of the application's private S3 bucket (a cloud storage container).
aws s3 ls s3://company-customer-data-bucket/
Why: This command asks the cloud to show all files in the bucket. If permissions are restricted, this should fail with 'Access Denied'.
12. Observe the output showing folders containing sensitive data such as 'invoices/', 'signed-contracts/', and 'id-documents/'.
Why: The successful listing proves the guest role has excessive permissions to view the structure of private customer data.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional travel app 'target.example' that lets users see 'Top Destinations' without logging in. The app's JavaScript contains an AWS Identity Pool ID. An attacker uses the AWS CLI to get guest credentials and runs 'aws s3 ls s3://target-storage/'. Because the developer attached the 'AmazonS3FullAccess' policy to the guest role instead of just allowing access to the '/public-images/' folder, the attacker can now see (and potentially download) a folder named '/user-passports/'. The vulnerability is not the public ID, but the 'FullAccess' permission given to anyone who uses that ID.
lesson.takeaway: Always inspect client-side JavaScript for AWS configuration details like Identity Pool IDs or User Pool IDs. While these IDs are not 'secrets' by themselves, they are the gateway to testing the permissions of the associated IAM roles. Use the AWS CLI to 'test the fences' by trying to list buckets, read database tables, or invoke functions. A common variant is finding these IDs in mobile app binaries (.ipa or .apk files). Avoid the mistake of reporting the ID itself as a leak; instead, prove that the ID grants access to data it shouldn't.
lesson.fix: Apply the Principle of Least Privilege to all IAM roles, especially unauthenticated ones. Instead of granting 's3:*' on an entire bucket, create a policy that only allows 's3:GetObject' on a specific public prefix. For example: { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "s3:GetObject", "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-bucket/public/*" }. Additionally, use IAM policy variables to ensure authenticated users can only access their own specific folders.

title: From P4 to P1 — Day 5: Open Redirect Vulnerabilities in Bug Bounty Hunting
summary_en: An open redirect vulnerability allows attackers to manipulate a website's navigation parameters to send users to malicious external domains. This can be used to make phishing attacks appear more credible by using a trusted domain as the starting point.

lesson.cause: The application accepts a destination URL from a user-controlled parameter, such as 'url' or 'next', and uses it in a redirect response without validation. This occurs because the server-side code blindly trusts the input provided in the HTTP request (a message sent from your browser to a server). Instead of checking if the destination is an internal path or an approved domain, the application places the untrusted input directly into the Location header ( the part of a server's response that tells the browser where to go). This lack of an allowlist (a list of approved safe items) creates a bridge for attackers to redirect users anywhere on the internet.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Browse the target application to find features that involve navigation, such as login, logout, or 'return to page' links.
2. Identify a URL (a web address) that contains a redirect-related parameter (a piece of data added to a URL after a '?').
https://example.com/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrusted.example
Why: We are looking for 'doorways' where the application asks the browser where it should go next.
DISCOVERY
3. Observe the original request to understand how the application normally behaves.
GET /redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrusted.example HTTP/1.1
Why: We need a baseline of a 'good' request to compare against our attack. (GET is a type of request used to retrieve data).
4. Use a tool like curl (a command-line program for sending web requests) to inspect the server's response headers.
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null 'https://example.com/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Ftrusted.example'
Why: We want to see the hidden instructions the server sends back to the browser.
5. Look for a 302 Found status code in the response.
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Why: A 302 status is the server's way of saying 'this page has moved, go to the address in the Location header'.
6. Verify the Location header matches the parameter value.
Location: https://trusted.example
Why: This confirms the application is using the 'url' parameter to decide where to send the user.
EXPLOITATION
7. Create a payload (malicious data) by replacing the trusted destination with an external site you control.
https://example.com/redirect?url=https://attacker.example
Why: We are testing if the application will blindly follow our instructions to leave its own domain.
8. Note that the URL uses URL encoding (translating special characters like / into %2F) to ensure the browser reads it correctly.
https://example.com/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Fattacker.example
Why: Proper formatting ensures the server processes the full address we provided.
9. Send the modified request to the server.
GET /redirect?url=https://attacker.example HTTP/1.1
Why: We are executing the test to see if the security gate is open.
IMPACT
10. Check the server's response for the new Location header.
Location: https://attacker.example
Why: If the server sends this header, it has successfully been tricked into redirecting the user to our site.
11. Test for weak validation by trying to trick simple filters, such as adding the trusted domain as a subdomain.
https://example.com/redirect?url=https://trusted.example.attacker.example
Why: Some apps only check if the 'trusted' name exists anywhere in the string, which is a common mistake.
12. Document the final result by showing that a user clicking a link on 'example.com' ends up on 'attacker.example'.
Final Destination: https://attacker.example
Why: This proves the vulnerability exists and demonstrates the potential for phishing.
lesson.example: Imagine a site called target.example that has a 'language switcher' feature. When you click a language, it redirects you back to the page you were on using a 'return_to' parameter. The vulnerable URL looks like this: https://target.example/set-lang?lang=en&return_to=/home. An attacker notices this and changes the 'return_to' parameter to an external site: https://target.example/set-lang?lang=en&return_to=https://evil-phishing-site.com. Because the server-side code simply takes whatever is in 'return_to' and puts it into a 'Location' header, the user's browser is automatically sent to the phishing site. The user might not notice because the link they clicked started with the trusted 'target.example' domain.
lesson.takeaway: Always look for parameters like 'next', 'redirect', 'url', and 'callback', especially in authentication flows like login or OAuth. A key signal is seeing a 302 or 301 redirect status code in your proxy history. A common variant is the 'folder bypass', where an attacker uses '../' to navigate out of intended directories. Avoid the mistake of assuming open redirects are always 'low' severity; if they can be used to leak sensitive tokens in an OAuth flow, they can become critical. Use automated scanners to find these parameters, but always manually verify if you can break out to an external domain like google.com.

title: I Didn’t Even Open Burp Suite — One URL Change Exposed Hidden WordPress Content
summary_en: A WordPress print endpoint let anyone retrieve private, draft, or pending posts by changing URL query parameters, exposing hidden content without authentication.

lesson.cause: The endpoint parses the full query string from the request (parse_str($url_data['query'], $args)) and then removes only the "print" argument. It passes the remaining arguments directly to WordPress's query_posts() function. Because query_posts() accepts parameters such as post_status, an attacker can set post_status=private, draft, or pending to force the database to return non‑public posts. The code never checks whether the requester is logged in or has permission to view those posts. Consequently, unauthenticated users can control the WP_Query arguments and read content that should be restricted.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify the target runs WordPress by looking at page source and common WP paths. Why: WordPress sites often expose predictable URLs (e.g., /wp‑admin, /wp‑content) which tells us the platform.
Step 2: Find a print‑related endpoint by browsing the site and noting URLs like /archives/123/?print=pdf. Why: The "print" query parameter suggests a feature that generates a printable version of a post.

DISCOVERY
Step 3: Open the URL in a browser and note the normal behaviour (PDF of public post). Why: Baseline shows the endpoint works for public content.
Step 4: Modify the URL to add extra parameters: ?print=print‑custom&post_status=private&posts_per_page=10. Payload: https://target.com/archives/123/?print=print‑custom&post_status=private&posts_per_page=10. Why: Adding "post_status=private" tells WordPress to query posts with status private; the endpoint does not filter this argument.
Step 5: Observe that the response now contains private posts even though no login occurred. Why: The server accepted the attacker‑controlled argument and returned the data.
Step 6: Repeat with post_status=draft and other statuses (pending) using similar URLs. Payload example: https://target.com/archives/123/?print=print‑custom&post_status=draft&posts_per_page=10. Why: Confirms the issue works for multiple non‑public states.

EXPLOITATION
Step 7: Review the server‑side code (shown in the article) that parses the query string: parse_str($url_data['query'], $args); unset($args['print']); if (!empty($args)) { $posts = query_posts($args); }. Why: Shows that after removing only "print", all other arguments are passed unchecked to query_posts().
Step 8: Realise that any WP_Query argument can be supplied, allowing enumeration of hidden content. Why: WP_Query supports many filters (author, category, post_type) which can be abused.

IMPACT
Step 9: Capture the returned HTML/PDF that contains private drafts. Why: Demonstrates the confidentiality breach – information that should be internal is now publicly accessible.
Step 10: Report the finding to the bug‑bounty program, noting that the issue is an access‑control flaw with high severity. Why: The impact includes potential leakage of confidential business data.
lesson.example: Imagine a site target.example that offers a printable view at /print.php?post=45&format=pdf. Vulnerable code: <?php $url = $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI']; $parts = parse_url($url); parse_str($parts['query'], $args); unset($args['format']); $posts = query_posts($args); ?> An attacker can request https://target.example/print.php?post=45&format=custom&post_status=private to retrieve a private post because the script passes the attacker‑controlled post_status to query_posts() without checking login. The URL is the payload; "post_status=private" tells WordPress to fetch private entries, and the script returns them because it never verifies the user.
lesson.takeaway: When testing WordPress or any CMS, look for endpoints that accept query parameters and then forward them to internal query functions. Search for patterns like parse_str(...); query_posts($args) or WP_Query($args) without an authentication check. Tools such as Burp Suite or a simple browser can be used to fuzz parameters like post_status, author, or post_type. Variants of this bug appear in custom plugins that expose search or export features. Beginners often forget to verify that the endpoint enforces user permissions before using user‑supplied arguments – always check for that missing check.
lesson.fix: Add an explicit authentication and capability check before processing any query arguments. For example: if (!is_user_logged_in() || !current_user_can('read_private_posts')) { wp_die('Unauthorized'); } Then whitelist only safe parameters (e.g., only "format") and discard others: $allowed = ['format']; foreach ($args as $key => $value) { if (!in_array($key, $allowed)) { unset($args[$key]); } } Finally, call query_posts() with the sanitized $args. This ensures unauthenticated users cannot influence WP_Query and only permitted data is returned.

title: How Stale Reset Tokens Led to Full Account Takeover (Even After Changing Email)
summary_en: A logic flaw allowed password reset tokens to remain valid after a user changed their email address, enabling full account takeover via the old email inbox.

lesson.cause: The application's password reset mechanism only checked if a token (a unique secret string used for identification) was expired or already used. It failed to verify if the account's primary email address had changed since the token was generated. Because the token was not 'bound' (permanently linked) to the specific email state at the time of creation, it remained 'stale' but functional, allowing anyone with access to the old email to hijack the account even after the user tried to secure it.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified the account management workflow, specifically how the application handles password resets and email updates.

DISCOVERY
2. Sign up for a new account using a primary email address, referred to as Email A.
3. Trigger the 'Forgot Password' feature for Email A to generate a reset token.
4. Receive the password-reset link in the inbox for Email A.
https://target.com/reset-password?token=unique_token_123
Why: This creates a 'token' (a secret code) that the server uses to identify which account is being reset without requiring a password.

EXPLOITATION
5. Before using the reset link, log into the account normally using the current credentials.
6. Navigate to the account settings (Settings -> General -> User account).
7. Change the account's registered email from Email A to a new address, Email B.
8. Save the changes and confirm that the account is now officially linked to Email B.
9. Open the original reset link that was sent to Email A in step 4.
https://target.com/reset-password?token=unique_token_123
Why: The researcher is testing if the server 'invalidates' (cancels) the old token when a sensitive security setting like the email address is changed.
10. Enter a new password into the reset form and submit the request.
POST /api/set-new-password HTTP/1.1
{"token": "unique_token_123", "password": "NewSecurePassword123!"}
Why: This sends the 'payload' (the data intended to exploit the flaw) to the server's 'endpoint' (the specific URL that processes password changes).

IMPACT
11. Observe that the application accepts the password change despite the token being 'stale' (issued before the email change).
12. Attempt to log in using the new email (Email B) and the password just set via the old token.
13. Confirm the login is successful, proving a full Account Takeover (ATO) is possible if an attacker has access to an old, abandoned, or compromised email inbox.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site 'target.example'. The site uses a database table for reset tokens that looks like this: {token: 'xyz', user_id: 1, expires: '2023-12-01'}. When a user changes their email, the site updates the 'users' table but forgets to delete entries in the 'reset_tokens' table. An attacker who previously gained access to the user's old email (Email A) finds a reset link from two days ago. Even though the user switched to Email B to stay safe, the attacker clicks the link. The server checks the 'reset_tokens' table, sees 'xyz' is still there and not expired, and allows the attacker to change the password for user_id 1. The attacker then logs in as the user using Email B and the new password.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for business logic flaws, always test the 'persistence' of security tokens across state changes. If a user changes their password, email, or enables Two-Factor Authentication (2FA), all previously issued tokens (reset links, session cookies, API keys) should be immediately 'invalidated' (made useless). Look for 'stale' tokens by performing an action, changing a setting, and then trying to complete the original action. A common mistake is only checking the expiration date of a token rather than its relationship to the current state of the account.

title: How I Earned 252.60 USDC from an ENS Bug
summary_en: A transfer flow in ENS Explorer updates the name’s ETH address before transferring ownership, so if the ownership transfer fails the address remains pointing to the recipient, allowing them to receive payments while the original owner still holds the name.

lesson.cause: The root cause is a mismatch between the UI’s displayed options (options) and the actual transaction builder (effectiveOptions). The UI hides the resolver‑detachment action because the owner lacks that permission, yet it still disables the ETH‑address field with an incorrect explanation. The transaction plan updates the ENS name’s ETH address first and then attempts the ownership transfer as two independent blockchain transactions. Because these transactions are not atomic, a failure in the second step leaves the address record changed while ownership stays with the original owner. This inconsistent state lets the recipient collect payments intended for the name’s owner.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Open the ENS Explorer transfer page in a browser. 
Why: The web page (UI) is the user interface that lets a user initiate name transfers.
Step 2: Observe that the "Detach resolver" checkbox is hidden (owner lacks permission) while the ETH‑address field is disabled with the note "Not needed while the resolver is being detached." 
Why: The UI reflects the owner’s permissions but shows a misleading explanation.

DISCOVERY
Step 3: Open the browser’s developer tools and watch the network requests when the transfer is submitted. 
Why: Network requests reveal the exact transactions the UI is sending to the blockchain.
Step 4: Notice two separate JSON payloads: one that calls the resolver’s setAddress function, and a second that calls the registrar’s transferFrom function. 
Why: The first payload updates the ENS name’s ETH address record; the second attempts to change name ownership. 

EXPLOITATION
Step 5: In the UI, enter a recipient address (e.g., 0xRecipient) and click "Transfer". 
Why: This triggers the two transactions described above.
Step 6: Payload sent to update the address (verbatim from the article – none provided, so left blank). 
Why: This transaction succeeds and writes the new ETH address into the ENS record.
Step 7: Payload sent to transfer ownership (verbatim – none provided). 
Why: This second transaction is expected to move the name to the recipient.
Step 8: As the recipient, cause the ownership transfer to revert (for example, by refusing to accept the name or by sending a transaction with insufficient gas). 
Why: A reverted transaction leaves the ownership unchanged but does not undo the earlier address update.
Step 9: Verify that the address update succeeded while the ownership transfer failed. 
Why: The blockchain state now shows the original owner still listed as the name’s owner, but the ETH address points to the recipient.

IMPACT
Step 10: Resolve the ENS name using any wallet (e.g., MetaMask) to retrieve the ETH address. 
Why: Resolution reads the resolver’s address record, which now contains the recipient’s address.
Step 11: Send a small amount of ETH to the ENS name. 
Why: The payment is routed to the address stored in the resolver, i.e., the recipient’s wallet.
Step 12: Confirm that the original owner can later restore the address record, but the earlier payment cannot be reclaimed. 
Why: The state inconsistency caused a one‑time loss of funds to the recipient while the name remained with the original owner.
lesson.takeaway: When reviewing smart‑contract or dApp workflows, always ask: if part of a multi‑step process fails, what state changes have already been committed? Look for UI elements that hide unavailable actions but still disable related fields with misleading text. Tools like transaction‑tracing, blockchain explorers, and network‑request inspection can reveal separate calls. Variants of this issue appear in token‑swap interfaces that approve a token before executing a trade, or in NFT marketplaces that update metadata before transferring ownership. Beginners often assume a UI button equals a single atomic operation; the key mistake is not verifying that the backend groups related state changes into one atomic transaction or rolls back on failure.
lesson.fix: The application should make the address update and ownership transfer an atomic operation: either both succeed or both revert. This can be done by a single smart‑contract function that first checks permissions, then updates the resolver’s address and transfers the name in one transaction, reverting on any error. The UI must generate the transaction plan from the same effective options it displays, ensuring the explanatory text matches the actual actions. Additionally, the UI should clearly show that the resolver will not be detached and should not disable the ETH‑address field with an unrelated message. By aligning the form’s `options` and `effectiveOptions` and using atomic contract calls, the inconsistent state is eliminated.

title: The User Was Removed. The Access Wasn’t.
summary_en: An API endpoint failed to verify if a user was still a member of a private project, allowing removed users to continue accessing sensitive project metadata and member lists.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a failure to distinguish between authentication and authorization at the /api/page/{pageId}/info endpoint. While the server correctly verified that the requester had a valid JWT (authentication), it did not check if that specific user still held permissions for the requested pageId (authorization). This logic flaw meant that any logged-in user with a known Page ID could retrieve its details, regardless of their membership status. The application likely assumed that if a user knew the ID, they must have access, or it simply failed to update its access control list (ACL) checks for this specific undocumented endpoint.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher examined the application's API documentation, which is a manual for how different parts of the software talk to each other.
2. They discovered an endpoint that was not being used by the visible website interface.
GET /api/page/{pageId}/info
Why: To find 'hidden' or undocumented functionality that might have weaker security than the main site.

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher logged into a test account to obtain a valid JWT, which is a digital ID card used to prove who a user is.
Authorization: Bearer <VALID_JWT>
Why: The API requires the user to be logged in (authenticated) before it will process any request.
4. They identified a Page ID, which is a unique number identifying a specific project page, by looking at the URL while they were still a member of that project.
/api/page/12345/info
Why: You need a valid target ID to see what information the server returns for a legitimate request.
5. They sent the request and observed a detailed response containing member emails, names, and permission levels.
{
 "name": "Private Project",
 "users": [{"email": "admin@example.com", "permissions": 500}]
}
Why: This establishes a baseline of what data is exposed by the endpoint.

EXPLOITATION
6. Using an administrator account, the researcher removed the test user from the project page.
Why: This simulates a real-world scenario where a user is fired or leaves a team and should no longer see private data.
7. The researcher sent the exact same request again using the removed user's JWT.
GET /api/page/12345/info HTTP/2
Host: <TARGET_HOST>
Authorization: Bearer <VALID_JWT>
Why: To see if the server checks if the user is still a member before sending the data.
8. The server responded with a 200 OK status, meaning the request was successful, and returned all the private project data.
Why: This proves the server only checks if the user is logged in, not if they are allowed to see this specific project.

IMPACT
9. The researcher updated the project members using the admin account while the user was still removed.
Why: To see if the removed user can see 'live' changes they were never supposed to know about.
10. The researcher requested the endpoint again and saw the new member list reflected in the response.
Why: This confirms the leak is not just cached (old) data, but a persistent, real-time unauthorized access to private information.
lesson.takeaway: Always test 'Access Revocation' scenarios: if a user is removed from a group, folder, or project, do their old links and API calls still work? When hunting, look for API documentation (like Swagger or Redoc) to find endpoints that the developers might have forgotten to secure as strictly as the main UI. A common mistake is relying on 'Security by Obscurity,' assuming that if a user doesn't see a button in the interface, they won't find the API endpoint. Variants of this bug include 'BOLA' (Broken Object Level Authorization), where you change an ID to see someone else's data, and 'Insecure Direct Object Reference' (IDOR).

title: How I Use AI to Find Potential IDOR Vulnerabilities: A Practical 6-Step Guide | by [Samadhan Shimple](https://samadhanshimple.medium.com/)
summary_en: A methodology for using AI to identify potential Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) parameters in HTTP requests, followed by manual verification using Burp Suite.

lesson.cause: The root cause is a failure in server-side authorization logic where the application trusts a client-provided identifier without verifying ownership. This happens when a developer assumes that an authenticated user should be able to access any resource they can name, failing to check if the user's session matches the resource's owner. In the article, endpoints like /api/orders/1001 are vulnerable because they rely solely on the ID provided in the request.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Create two separate test accounts, Account A and Account B, to act as the attacker and the victim.
2. Use Burp Suite, a tool for intercepting and inspecting web traffic, to capture HTTP requests (messages sent from your browser to a server).
3. Browse the application to find features that read or update data, looking for endpoints (specific web addresses that perform tasks) like /api/users/123.
DISCOVERY
4. Identify parameters, which are specific pieces of information sent in a request, that look like database IDs.
5. Prepare a sanitized HTTP request by removing sensitive data like cookies (small files used to keep you logged in) or passwords.
6. Use an AI prompt to analyze the request: "Analyze the following sanitized HTTP request for potential broken access control and IDOR risks."
7. Review the AI's suggestions for common IDOR candidates like user_id, account_id, or document_id.
EXPLOITATION
8. Check the URL path, the part of the address after the site name, for IDs: GET /api/users/123
Why: The number 123 identifies a specific user profile (an object reference).
9. Check query parameters, extra details added after a question mark in a URL: GET /api/documents?document_id=456
Why: The document_id tells the server which file to fetch (a query-based reference).
10. Check the JSON body, a structured data format used in requests: {"document_id": 456, "title": "Test"}
Why: The server might use the ID inside the data list to decide which record to update (a body-based reference).
11. Use Burp Suite Repeater, a tool to modify and re-send requests, to take a request from Account A and replace the ID with one belonging to Account B.
IMPACT
12. Send the modified request and observe if the server returns Account B's private data to Account A.
Why: If the server returns the data, it proves it is not checking if Account A actually owns that ID (successful IDOR).
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site called target.example that lets users view their private medical reports. When a user clicks 'View Report', the browser sends this request: GET /api/v1/reports/view?report_id=8821. The server-side code looks like this: report = database.query("SELECT * FROM reports WHERE id = " + request.params.report_id); return report;. This code is vulnerable because it fetches the report based only on the ID provided by the user. An attacker logged in as User A can change the report_id to 8822 (User B's report). Because the code never checks if the logged-in user's ID matches the 'owner_id' column in the database, User A will successfully see User B's private medical information.
lesson.takeaway: Always look for parameters that appear to be database keys or resource names, even if they aren't simple numbers. Use AI to quickly scan large amounts of traffic for these patterns, but never trust AI to confirm the bug; manual testing with two accounts is mandatory. A common variant is finding IDs in custom HTTP headers (metadata sent with requests) or nested inside complex JSON objects. A beginner mistake is assuming that long, random-looking IDs (UUIDs) are safe; they are still vulnerable if the server doesn't check ownership.
lesson.fix: The server must implement an authorization check for every request that accesses a resource. Instead of just querying by the ID, the query should include the authenticated user's ID. For example, in Node.js: app.get('/api/reports/:id', (req, res) => { const reportId = req.params.id; const userId = req.session.userId; db.query('SELECT * FROM reports WHERE id = ? AND owner_id = ?', [reportId, userId], (err, result) => { if (result.length === 0) return res.status(403).send('Unauthorized'); res.json(result); }); });

title: Breaking the Vault: Bypassing Chatbot Limits via Race Conditions & Response Manipulation
summary_en: An attacker bypassed a 5-conversation chatbot limit by using a race condition to generate extra session IDs and manipulating server responses to trick the frontend. This allowed for unlimited resource consumption and a potential Denial of Wallet attack against the provider's AI infrastructure.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) flaw where the server checks the conversation count in the database without using atomic operations or locks. This allows multiple requests sent at the exact same millisecond to pass the check simultaneously. Additionally, the application relied on client-side state for UI enforcement and failed to re-verify session validity when the frontend was tricked into accepting a manually injected conversation ID.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified a business rule limiting users to 5 active chatbot conversations in the UI (User Interface: the buttons and menus you see on screen).
2. The researcher opened the browser's network tools to identify the endpoint (a specific web address that performs a task) responsible for starting new chats.
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher created 4 conversations to reach the threshold where the next request would be the limit.
4. The researcher prepared to send the 5th request while using Burp Suite (a tool used to catch and change web traffic between a browser and a server).
EXPLOITATION (PHASE 1: RACE CONDITION)
5. The researcher intercepted the request to initialize a new conversation.
POST /redacted/api/v1/chatbot/conversations/init HTTP/2
Host: redacted.com
{"platform":"website"}
Why: This HTTP request (a message sent from your computer to a server) tells the backend (the hidden part of the website that processes data) to start a new chat.
6. The researcher sent this request to Turbo Intruder, a tool designed to send many requests at the exact same time.
7. The researcher configured the tool to fire 5 identical requests simultaneously.
8. The researcher observed that the server returned multiple success messages instead of just one.
HTTP/2 200 OK
Why: 200 OK is a status code (a number from a server) meaning the request worked. The server checked the database (a digital filing cabinet) for all 5 requests before any of them finished updating the count.
9. The researcher saved one of the extra "conversation_id" values (a unique token identifying a chat) generated by these successful requests.
EXPLOITATION (PHASE 2: FRONTEND BYPASS)
10. The researcher refreshed the page and saw the "New Conversation" button was disabled because the UI correctly counted 5+ chats.
11. The researcher intercepted the request used to fetch the list of active chats.
GET /redacted/api/v1/chatbot/conversations HTTP/2
Why: This request asks the server for the data the browser uses to decide if the "New" button should be clickable.
12. The researcher viewed the server's response, which contained a JSON array (a list of data items) of the active chats.
13. The researcher deleted one chat object from the list in the intercepted response.
14. The researcher forwarded the modified response to the browser.
15. The researcher observed the "New Conversation" button was now enabled because the browser was tricked into thinking only 4 chats existed.
EXPLOITATION (PHASE 3: BACKEND BYPASS)
16. The researcher clicked the "New Conversation" button to trigger a fresh creation request.
17. The server correctly rejected the request because the database knew the real count was too high.
HTTP/2 429 Too Many Requests
Why: A 429 error is a status code meaning the user has exceeded a rate or quantity limit.
18. The researcher intercepted this 429 error response before the browser could process it.
19. The researcher changed the status code from "429" to "200 OK".
20. The researcher replaced the error message in the response body with a fake success message.
21. The researcher injected the "conversation_id" saved from Step 9 into this fake message.
{"status": "success", "conversation_id": "[RACE_CONDITION_ID]", "message": "User registered..."}
Why: This tricks the frontend into believing the server successfully created a new, valid chat session.
IMPACT
22. The researcher opened the new chat window and sent a message.
23. The researcher confirmed the backend processed the message using the injected ID, proving the limit was bypassed.
24. The researcher concluded this could lead to a Denial of Wallet (DoW) attack, where an attacker drains the company's money by forcing their AI to process thousands of unauthorized, expensive requests.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always look for features with strict numerical limits, such as 'Max 3 files,' 'One coupon per user,' or '5 free searches.' Use tools like Burp Suite's 'Send group in parallel' to test if the server can handle multiple requests at the exact same time without losing count. A common mistake is assuming that if the frontend (the browser) blocks an action, the backend (the server) is safe; always try to manipulate the server's responses to see if the frontend can be tricked into performing unauthorized actions. Variants of this bug include 'double-spending' in financial apps or 'double-voting' in polls.
lesson.fix: To fix this, the backend must use atomic database operations or row-level locking to ensure that the 'check' and 'update' steps happen as a single, unbreakable unit. Instead of checking the count and then updating it in two steps, use a single SQL query: 'UPDATE users SET chat_count = chat_count + 1 WHERE user_id = ? AND chat_count < 5;'. If the count is already 5, the database will update zero rows, and the application can safely return an error. Additionally, the backend should never trust a conversation ID provided by the client unless it has been strictly validated against the user's current session state.

title: Insufficient Session Expiration leads to Account Takeover via Password Change
summary_en: A session management flaw allowed an attacker to use an expired session token to change a user's password, leading to full account takeover. The platform failed to invalidate tokens upon logout and did not require the current password for security updates.

lesson.cause: The root cause is insufficient session expiration, where the server fails to invalidate (make unusable) a session token (a secret key identifying a user) after logout. This occurred on the presentation platform's profile and password change endpoints (specific web addresses for tasks). The backend code accepted the 'auth_token' parameter (a piece of data in a request) regardless of whether the user had officially logged out. Furthermore, the password change feature lacked a requirement for the 'old password' or 2FA (an extra security code). This allowed a 24-hour window for an attacker to reuse a captured token to gain full control.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher logged into the presentation platform and captured the session token (a secret key identifying the user).
auth_token=abk193
Why: To identify the parameter (a piece of data in a request) used for authentication (proving who you are).
2. The researcher navigated to the user profile page to test for access control (rules about who can see what).
GET /user/profile HTTP/1.1
Why: To find an endpoint (a specific URL for a task) where user data can be modified.
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher attempted to change the account name using a token from a different account.
auth_token=[attacker_token]
Why: To test if the system properly checks if the token belongs to the account being changed.
4. The researcher observed that the name change was successful, indicating an initial access control flaw.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Why: This confirmed the server was not strictly validating the relationship between the token and the specific user data.
5. The researcher logged out of the account to end the session (a temporary connection).
GET /logout HTTP/1.1
Why: To trigger the invalidation (making a token unusable) process on the server side.
6. The researcher logged back in to generate a new, active session token.
auth_token=[new_token]
Why: To establish a baseline for what a 'valid' current token looks like.
7. The researcher attempted to use the old token to change the name again.
auth_token=abk193
Why: To see if the server still accepts the token after logout, which is a sign of insufficient session expiration.
8. The researcher confirmed the name changed successfully using the old token.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Why: This proved the server does not delete or blacklist tokens from its database when a user logs out.
EXPLOITATION
9. The researcher navigated to the password change feature to increase the impact of the bug.
POST /change-password HTTP/1.1
Why: To target a high-impact feature that could lead to Account Takeover (gaining full control of an account).
10. The researcher entered a new password in the form fields provided by the platform.
new_password=attacker_pass&confirm_password=attacker_pass
Why: To prepare the payload (the actual data being sent) for the password change request.
11. The researcher captured the password change request and replaced the active token with the old victim token.
Cookie: auth_token=abk193
Why: To exploit the fact that the server still considers the old token valid for critical actions.
12. The researcher sent the modified request to the server.
POST /change-password HTTP/1.1
Why: To execute the final step of the exploit and change the victim's password.
IMPACT
13. The researcher observed that the server accepted the old token and updated the password.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Why: This confirmed that the password change endpoint lacks security protections like requiring the 'old password'.
14. The researcher logged out and successfully logged back in using the victim's email and the new password.
Login: victim@example.com / attacker_pass
Why: To prove a permanent Account Takeover (ATO) was achieved.
15. The researcher noted that the token remained valid for over 24 hours.
Validity: > 24 hours
Why: To demonstrate the long window of opportunity an attacker has to use a stolen token.
16. The researcher concluded that even if a victim clicks 'Logout', an attacker with the token maintains access.
Impact: Critical
Why: Because the server-side session is never truly destroyed until a long timeout occurs.
lesson.example: Imagine a site target.example where you log in and get a cookie 'session_id=xyz'. When you click 'Logout', the site deletes the cookie from your browser, but the server still has 'xyz' marked as 'active' in its database. An attacker who stole 'xyz' earlier can send a request: 'POST /account/email-update HTTP/1.1' with 'Cookie: session_id=xyz' and 'new_email=hacker@evil.com'. Because the server doesn't check if the user actually logged out or ask for the current password, it changes the email. Now the attacker can use the 'Forgot Password' feature to send a reset link to hacker@evil.com and take over the account. This works because the server failed to 'invalidate' (kill) the session on its end.
lesson.takeaway: Always test if session tokens (secret keys for sessions) remain functional after a logout or a password change. Look for critical endpoints (specific URLs for tasks) like 'change email' or 'change password' that do not require the user to enter their current password. Use tools like Burp Suite to capture a token, log out, and then try to reuse that token in a 'Repeater' request. A common variant is 'Session Fixation', where an attacker forces a specific token on a victim. A beginner mistake is assuming that because a cookie is gone from the browser, it is also gone from the server's memory.
lesson.fix:
To fix this, the server must implement strict session management. First, when a user logs out, the server must invalidate the session token in its database so it can never be used again. Second, when a password is changed, the server should automatically kill all other active sessions for that user. Third, critical actions like changing a password must require the user to provide their 'current password' or a 2FA code. Finally, tokens should have a short expiration time. 

```python
def logout_user(session_token):
    # CORRECT: Delete the session from the server-side store
    db.execute('DELETE FROM active_sessions WHERE token = ?', (session_token,))
    return 'Logged out successfully'
```

title: Private Bug Bounty Experience— Tata Play Bug Bounty Program
summary_en: An unauthenticated Spring Boot Actuator interface was exposed on a Tata Play subdomain, revealing sensitive infrastructure details and management endpoints like /shutdown.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by a misconfiguration in the Spring Boot framework where management endpoints, designed for internal monitoring, were exposed to the public internet. By default, Spring Boot Actuator provides several 'endpoints' (specific web addresses used for monitoring) that can reveal system health, environment variables, or even allow remote application shutdown if not explicitly secured with authentication (a login process).
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher performed reconnaissance (the process of gathering information about a target) on Tata Play's subdomains to find interesting web services.

DISCOVERY
2. The researcher identified a subdomain running a Java-based application and attempted to access the Actuator index (a directory of management tools).
3. The researcher sent a GET request (a standard message used by browsers to ask a server for a page) to the following endpoint:
GET /actuator HTTP/1.1
Why: This request asks the server to list all available management functions. (An endpoint is a specific URL path that performs a task).
4. The server responded with an HTTP 200 OK status ( a code meaning the request was successful) and a JSON body (a structured text format used for data exchange).
5. The JSON response contained a list of links, including sensitive ones like "shutdown" and "refresh".
6. The researcher then checked the health endpoint to see what information it revealed.
7. The researcher sent the following request:
GET /actuator/health HTTP/1.1
Why: This endpoint is used to check if the application is running, but it often leaks details about the underlying infrastructure like database status.
8. The server returned detailed information about the application's internal health and infrastructure components.

EXPLOITATION
9. The researcher noted the presence of the shutdown endpoint:
"shutdown": { "href": "https://[redacted]/actuator/shutdown", "templated": false }
Why: This indicates that the application might allow an unauthenticated user to stop the entire service. (Unauthenticated means the user has not logged in).
10. The researcher followed ethical guidelines and did not attempt to trigger the shutdown, as this would cause a Denial of Service (an attack that makes a service unavailable to users).
11. The researcher observed that while some endpoints returned an HTTP 403 Forbidden (a code meaning access is denied), the main index and health data remained public.

IMPACT
12. The researcher documented the findings, showing that an attacker could gain deep knowledge of the server's setup or potentially crash the application.
lesson.example:
Imagine a fictional company 'target.example' that uses Spring Boot for its backend. A researcher finds that the developers forgot to secure the management tools. 

1. The researcher visits: https://api.target.example/actuator/env
2. The server responds with a list of all environment variables (settings used by the app).
3. Inside the response, the researcher finds: "DB_PASSWORD": "SuperSecret123!"
4. This happens because the 'env' endpoint (which shows environment settings) was not restricted to administrators. 

An attacker could now use this password to log into the company's database and steal user data.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always check for common framework-specific paths like '/actuator', '/heapdump', or '/env' on Java applications. Use automated scanners or wordlists (lists of common file names) to find these hidden management interfaces. A key signal is finding a server that returns a JSON list of links when you visit '/actuator'. A common mistake is assuming that if the main '/actuator' page is blocked, the sub-pages are also blocked; always test individual endpoints like '/actuator/health' or '/actuator/info' separately.
lesson.fix:
To fix this, developers should use Spring Security to ensure that all actuator endpoints require a valid administrator login. Additionally, sensitive endpoints like 'shutdown' should be disabled entirely if not needed. In the 'application.properties' file, you can restrict exposure using the following configuration:

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
management.endpoint.health.show-details=never
management.endpoint.shutdown.enabled=false

This configuration ensures only basic health and info are visible, details are hidden, and the shutdown command is completely turned off.

title: How I found BAC leads to De-escalate the Administrator privilege
summary_en: A low-privileged user can strip an administrator of their permissions by sending them a team invitation, which triggers a logic error that downgrades the admin's account to a 'pending' state.

lesson.cause: The application's invitation logic failed to verify if an email address was already associated with an active, high-privileged account before processing a new invite. When the 'Internal User' (attacker) sent an invitation to the 'Administrator' (victim) at victim@gmail.com, the system likely updated the existing user record's status to 'pending' or 'invited.' This design flaw allowed a subordinate to overwrite the state of a superior account, effectively performing an unauthorized privilege de-escalation.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify the hierarchy of roles within the organization-based application.
Code: Administrator (Full Control), Internal User (Limited), External User (N/A)
Why: To understand the target (Administrator) and the attacker's starting position (Internal User). A Role is a set of permissions assigned to a user.

DISCOVERY
Step 2: Locate the user invitation feature available to the 'Internal User' role.
Code: [Invitation Functionality]
Why: This is the target endpoint where the vulnerability resides. An Endpoint is a specific web address or 'door' on a server where a function lives.

EXPLOITATION
Step 3: Identify the email address of the target Administrator.
Code: victim@gmail.com
Why: The email serves as the unique identifier for the account the attacker wants to disrupt.

Step 4: Use the 'Internal User' account to send a new invitation to the Administrator's email address.
Code: attacker@gmail.com invites victim@gmail.com
Why: The researcher is testing if the system allows 're-inviting' an existing user. A Parameter is a piece of information, like an email, sent to the server to process.

IMPACT
Step 5: Log in as the Administrator to check the account status.
Code: [Administrator Dashboard]
Why: To see if the invitation affected the existing account. The UI (User Interface) is the visual part of the website you click and see.

Step 6: Observe that administrative control buttons have vanished from the Administrator's view.
Code: "The buttons of accepting and ignoring had disappeared"
Why: The system processed the invite and downgraded the Admin's active session to a restricted 'pending' state. This is Privilege De-escalation, a bug where a user's power is reduced by an unauthorized person.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for logic bugs, always test how 'Invite' or 'Add User' features handle emails that are already registered in the system. Look for instances where a system 'updates' an existing record instead of 'rejecting' the duplicate input. A common signal is when an app allows you to 're-send' an invite to someone who is already a member. A variant of this bug involves 'Self-Registration' where signing up with an existing admin's email might trigger a password reset or account merge. Avoid the mistake of assuming that 'Invite' forms only create new records; they often interact with existing ones.
